[[StackCanary|canary]] / [[AddressSpaceLayoutRandomization|ASLR]] / [[ExecutableSpaceProtection|NX]] / [[ReturnOrientedProgramming|ROP]] ([[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow|Ch 7.10]]) — operationalizes [[dis-0-introduction|Ch 0]]'s *active-reading-by-typing-the-code* pedagogy at the assembly surface. **Structural sibling of [[dis-1-8-exercises|Ch 1.8]] / [[dis-2-11-exercises|Ch 2.11]] / [[dis-4-10-exercises|Ch 4.10]] / [[dis-5-11-exercises|Ch 5.11]]** — exercise-set-closes-chapter pattern. **76th ingested DIS chapter — fully completes Ch 7 *64-bit x86 Assembly*.** No new concept pages — pure problem-set close.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 7.6 Recursion (x86-64)](sources/dis-7-6-x86-64-recursion.md) — **Sixth leaf** of Ch 7 *x86-64 Assembly* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]*. Applies the [[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions|Ch 7.5]] function-call apparatus ([[CallInstruction|`callq`]] / [[RetInstruction|`retq`]] / [[LeaveInstruction|`leaveq`]] + [[CallingConvention|System V calling convention]] + [[FramePointer|`%rbp`]]-anchored [[StackFrame|stack frames]]) to the **self-invoking** case via the [[Recursion|recursive]] `sumr(n)` worked example (sum from `n` down to 1). Headline rule: *"each recursive call generates a new stack frame"* — recursion adds **no new instructions** at the [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] level, just a **dynamic-call-chain pattern** on top of Ch 7.5's mechanism. Recursion depth $d$ ⇒ $d + 1$ live `sumr` frames stacked along the [[CallStack|call stack]] at the deepest point — the **structural memory cost** of recursive algorithms. Base case (`n <= 0` → return 0) vs recursive case (`n + sumr(n-1)`) realized as a standard [[AsmIfThenElse|Ch 7.4.2]] if-pattern — [[CmpInstruction|`cmp`]] of `n` against `0`, [[X86JumpInstructions|`jg`]] on the negated condition (the *"jumps when condition is not true"* rule). The recursive [[CallInstruction|`callq sumr`]] is **structurally identical** to any other `callq` — the [[CallingConvention|calling convention]] (`%edi` = 1st param, `%eax` = return) applies on every invocation; the [[FramePointer|`%rbp`]]-anchored frame discipline is re-established on every entry. Return-value flow: the recursive `callq` deposits `sumr(n-1)` into `%eax`, then `add -0x4(%rbp), %eax` folds the local `n` into the running accumulator before `leaveq; retq` unwinds the frame. **Scope notes**: [[TailRecursion|tail-call optimization]] and stack-overflow / depth-limits are **not** covered — the `sumr` example is **not** tail-recursive (the `add` after the recursive call keeps it out of tail position) and the chapter does not address what happens when the [[CallStack|call stack]] runs out of room. **71st ingested DIS chapter — sixth leaf of Ch 7.** Mints **1 new concept page** ([[Recursion]] — promoted from forward-reference; the [[ComputerScience|CS]] concept now operationalized at the [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] level) + **promotes 1 forward reference** ([[CallStack]] — first referenced by [[dis-7-2-x86-64-common|Ch 7.2]]'s `adder2` trace and used heavily by [[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions|Ch 7.5]] / [[StackPointer]] / [[X86StackInstructions]] / [[CallInstruction]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 7.5 Functions in Assembly (x86-64)](sources/dis-7-5-x86-64-functions.md) — **Fifth leaf** of Ch 7 *x86-64 Assembly* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]*. Closes the per-ISA tour by adding the **function-call instruction family** ([[CallInstruction|`callq`]] / [[RetInstruction|`retq`]] / [[LeaveInstruction|`leaveq`]]) on top of the [[dis-7-1-x86-64-basics|register/operand]] / [[dis-7-2-x86-64-common|data-movement/stack]] / [[dis-7-3-x86-64-arithmetic|arithmetic]] / [[dis-7-4-x86-64-conditional-loops|control-flow]] surface assembled by 7.1–7.4. Operationalizes the **System V AMD64 [[CallingConvention|calling convention]]** at the [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] level: the **six argument registers** (`%rdi` / `%rsi` / `%rdx` / `%rcx` / `%r8` / `%r9` for params 1–6, stack for 7+); `%rax` as the return-value register; the [[StackPointer|`%rsp` invariant]] (*"always points to the top of the stack"*) and the [[FramePointer|`%rbp` invariant]] (*"points to the base of the current stack frame"*); and the [[CallerSavedRegister|caller-saved]] vs [[CalleeSavedRegister|callee-saved]] partition (`%rax`/`%rcx`/`%rdx`/`%rsi`/`%rdi`/`%r8`–`%r11` caller-owned vs `%rbx`/`%rbp`/`%r12`–`%r15` callee-owned). Canonical prologue (`push %rbp; mov %rsp, %rbp; sub $N, %rsp`) / epilogue ([[LeaveInstruction|`leaveq`]] = *"equivalent to `mov %rbp, %rsp` then `pop %rbp`"* + [[RetInstruction|`retq`]]) pattern formalized. **70th ingested DIS chapter — fifth leaf of Ch 7.** Mints **6 new concept pages** ([[CallInstruction]], [[RetInstruction]], [[LeaveInstruction]], [[CallingConvention]], [[CallerSavedRegister]], [[CalleeSavedRegister]]) plus **promotes 2 forward references** ([[StackPointer]], [[FramePointer]] — first flagged in [[dis-7-2-x86-64-common|Ch 7.2]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 7.8 Matrices in Assembly (x86-64)](sources/dis-7-8-x86-64-matrices.md) — **Eighth leaf** of Ch 7 *x86-64 Assembly* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **matrices extension** of [[dis-7-7-x86-64-arrays|Ch 7.7]]'s 1-D array-compilation pattern to the 2-D case. Walks two [[CLanguage|C]] [[MultidimensionalArray|2-D-array]] layouts at the [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] surface: **contiguous** (statically declared `int M1[4][3]` or single-`malloc` `int *M3 = malloc(ROWS*COLS*sizeof(int))` — *"all the rows contiguously in memory"* in [[RowMajorOrder|row-major order]]) where element `M[i][j]` collapses to a single linear `i*cols + j` offset using the [[AsmArrayAccess|Ch 7.7 scaled-index pattern]] with [[LeaInstruction|`lea 0x0(,%rax,4),%rdx`]] materializing the `(i*cols+j)*4` offset (*"multiply (i*cols+j) by 4, put in %rdx"*); and **[[ArrayOfArrays|noncontiguous array-of-arrays]]** (`int **matrix` — *"each row is allocated contiguously in memory, but separate rows are not necessarily contiguous with one another"*) where access requires **two scaled-multiplies + two memory loads** (*"multiply i by 8, place in %rdx"* for the row pointer at scale 8, then *"multiply j by 4, place in %rdx"* inside the row at scale 4). Headline rule: the **layout choice is observable at the assembly surface** — contiguous = one memory load per element; noncontiguous = two-stage pointer chase + worse cache behavior. **No new instructions** — reuses [[X86MovInstruction|`mov`]], [[LeaInstruction|`lea`]], [[X86MulInstruction|`imul`]], and [[ScaledIndexAddressing|scaled-index addressing]]; the novelty is the **compilation pattern** that realizes the [[dis-2-5-arrays|Ch 2.5]] source-level layout distinction at the [[X86_64|x86-64]] level. **73rd ingested DIS chapter — eighth leaf of Ch 7.** Mints **0 new concept pages** — the existing [[MultidimensionalArray]] / [[RowMajorOrder]] / [[ArrayOfArrays]] / [[AsmArrayAccess]] machinery covers the new content.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 7.4.3 Loops in Assembly (x86-64)](sources/dis-7-4-3-x86-64-loops.md) — **Third and final leaf** of [[dis-7-4-x86-64-conditional-loops|Ch 7.4]] of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]*. Operationalizes the [[dis-7-4-1-x86-64-preliminaries|Ch 7.4.1]] mechanism families ([[X86FlagsRegister|FLAGS]] + [[CmpInstruction|`cmp`]] + [[X86JumpInstructions|conditional jumps]]) into the **canonical compilation pattern** for [[CLanguage|C]]'s [[WhileLoop|`while`]] / [[ForLoop|`for`]] / [[DoWhileLoop|`do`–`while`]] constructs at the [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] surface, via a single worked example — `sumUp(int n)`. Headline rules: (1) the **canonical `while`/`for` pattern** is **jump-to-test** — an unconditional `jmp` skips the body, lands at the condition check, and a conditional jump on the **un-negated** loop condition branches **back** to the body — the **inverse** of [[AsmIfThenElse|Ch 7.4.2]]'s if-pattern (forward jump on the **negated** condition); (2) `for` and `while` produce **identical assembly** — *"every `for` loop can be represented by a `while` loop"* — `for (init; cond; step) { body; }` decomposes mechanically to `init; while (cond) { body; step; }`; (3) `do`–`while` **drops the leading `jmp`** because the body always executes once unconditionally — *"test conditions typically execute before the body (except do-while)"* — making the do-while pattern strictly simpler at the assembly surface. **69th ingested DIS chapter — third and final leaf of [[dis-7-4-x86-64-conditional-loops|Ch 7.4]], closing the [[ControlFlow|control-flow]] section of Ch 7.** Mints **1 new concept page** ([[AsmLoopPattern]] — the canonical jump-to-test loop compilation pattern covering all three of `while` / `for` / `do`–`while`).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 7.4.2 If Statements in Assembly (x86-64)](sources/dis-7-4-2-x86-64-if-statements.md) — **Second leaf** of [[dis-7-4-x86-64-conditional-loops|Ch 7.4]] of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]*. Operationalizes the [[dis-7-4-1-x86-64-preliminaries|Ch 7.4.1]] mechanism families ([[X86FlagsRegister|FLAGS]] + [[CmpInstruction|`cmp`]] + [[X86JumpInstructions|conditional jumps]]) into the **canonical compilation pattern** for [[CLanguage|C]]'s [[IfStatement|`if`]] / [[ElseStatement|`else`]] construct via a single worked example — `getSmallest(int x, int y)` — traced through both **unoptimized (branch-based)** and **`-O1`-optimized (branch-free, [[X86ConditionalMove|`cmov`]]-based)** [[X86_64|x86-64]] assembly. Two headline rules: (1) the branch-based form jumps on the **negated** source condition (*"a standard if statement [is] where a jump occurs when conditions are **not** true"*) — the [[X86JumpInstructions|`jle`]] in the `getSmallest` trace fires precisely when `x ≤ y`, falling through to the then-branch when the source `x > y` holds; (2) the `-O1` substitution to [[X86ConditionalMove|`cmov`]] (*"`cmov` executes both conditional branches in hardware, selecting the result afterward"*) **eliminates** the [[ControlHazard|control hazard]] / [[BranchPrediction|branch-prediction]] dependency from [[dis-5-8-pipelining-advanced|Ch 5.8]] entirely — at the cost of requiring both arms to be safely pre-evaluable (*"the compiler takes the safe road and uses jumps"* when [[NullPointerSafety|null-pointer dereference]] or side effects make pre-evaluation unsafe). **68th ingested DIS chapter — second leaf of [[dis-7-4-x86-64-conditional-loops|Ch 7.4]].** Mints **3 new concept pages** ([[X86ConditionalMove]], [[AsmIfThenElse]], [[BranchInstruction]] — last one promoted from forward-reference).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 7.4.1 Preliminaries (x86-64 Conditional Control)](sources/dis-7-4-1-x86-64-preliminaries.md) — **First leaf** of [[dis-7-4-x86-64-conditional-loops|Ch 7.4]] of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]*. Introduces the three mechanisms every conditional construct at the [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] level rests on: the **[[X86FlagsRegister|FLAGS condition-code register]]** (the single-bit ALU side-channel — ZF / SF / OF / CF), the **comparison instructions [[CmpInstruction|`cmp`]] and [[TestInstruction|`test`]]** (set flags *without* writing a destination — flag-only siblings of [[X86ArithmeticInstructions|`sub`]] and [[X86BitwiseInstructions|`and`]] respectively), and the **[[X86JumpInstructions|jump-instruction family]]** (`jmp` unconditional + signed `je`/`jne`/`jg`/`jge`/`jl`/`jle` and unsigned `ja`/`jae`/`jb`/`jbe` conditional jumps). Headline rules: (1) the **same** [[CmpInstruction|`cmp`]] sets **all four flags** — the signed/unsigned split lives entirely in the **consumer** mnemonic (`g`/`l` consume SF + OF; `a`/`b` consume CF), realizing the bit-pattern-interpretation-invariance from [[dis-4-3-signed|Ch 4.3]] / [[dis-4-5-overflow|Ch 4.5]] at the instruction surface; (2) the **`test %rax, %rax`** idiom is the canonical register-zero test (`x AND x = 0` iff `x = 0`); (3) jump instructions are the **indirect channel** through which [[InstructionPointer|`%rip`]] changes — restating [[dis-7-1-x86-64-basics|Ch 7.1]]'s *"`%rip` is read-only — cannot be written directly"* rule. **67th ingested DIS chapter — first leaf of [[dis-7-4-x86-64-conditional-loops|Ch 7.4]].** Mints **5 new concept pages** ([[X86FlagsRegister]], [[ConditionCode]], [[CmpInstruction]], [[TestInstruction]], [[X86JumpInstructions]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 7.10 Buffer Overflows (x86-64)](sources/dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow.md) — **Tenth leaf** of Ch 7 *x86-64 Assembly* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **security payoff** of the whole Ch 7 stack-discipline tour. Fuses [[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions|Ch 7.5]]'s [[CallStack|call-stack]] mechanics ([[CallInstruction|`callq`]] / [[RetInstruction|`retq`]] / [[StackFrame|stack frames]] / [[FramePointer|`%rbp`]]) with the [[CArray|C-array]] / [[CString|string]] vulnerabilities flagged in [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]] / [[dis-2-6-strings|Ch 2.6]] into the canonical [[StackSmashing|stack-smashing]] exploit: an unbounded `scanf("%s", buf)` writes past a 12-byte buffer, overwrites the saved return address at `8(%rbp)`, and on [[RetInstruction|`retq`]] redirects [[InstructionPointer|`%rip`]] into attacker-chosen code. Walks the `secret` worked example with a precise 48-byte payload (**40 bytes of padding + 8-byte little-endian address `0x4006da`**). Three defense layers: programmer-level ([[BoundsChecking|length-specifying functions]] — `fgets` / `scanf("%12s")` / [[Strncpy|`strncpy`]] / `strncat` / `snprintf`), compiler / OS-level ([[StackCanary|stack canaries]], [[AddressSpaceLayoutRandomization|ASLR]], [[ExecutableSpaceProtection|NX / DEP]]), and **why each is bypassable** ([[ReturnOrientedProgramming|ROP]] defeats NX; canaries can be overwritten with the original value; ASLR can be brute-forced or sidestepped by NOP sleds). Closes with the **Morris Worm (1988)** ([[Daemon|`fingerd`]] overrun) and **AOL Chat Wars** case studies. Headline quote: *"The C language does not perform automatic array bounds checking"*. **75th ingested DIS chapter — tenth leaf of Ch 7.** Mints **7 new concept pages** ([[StackSmashing]], [[ReturnAddressOverwrite]], [[StackCanary]], [[AddressSpaceLayoutRandomization]], [[ExecutableSpaceProtection]], [[ReturnOrientedProgramming]], [[Daemon]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 7.9 Structs in Assembly (x86-64)](sources/dis-7-9-x86-64-structs.md) — **Ninth leaf** of Ch 7 *x86-64 Assembly* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]*. Shows how the [[CLanguage|C]] [[CStruct|struct]] aggregate compiles to [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] — fields stored **contiguously in declaration order**, accessed via fixed compile-time `disp(%base)` offsets ([[X86MovInstruction|`mov %edx, 0x44(%rax)`]] writes `grad_yr` 68 bytes past struct base). Codifies the [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AlignmentRule|alignment rule]] — *"x64's alignment policy requires that two-byte data types (i.e., `short`) reside at a two-byte-aligned address, four-byte data types (i.e., `int`, `float`, and `unsigned`) reside at four-byte-aligned addresses, and larger data types (`long`, `double`, and pointer data) reside at eight-byte-aligned addresses"* — and the [[CCompiler|compiler]]-inserted [[StructPadding|padding]] mechanism — *"the compiler adds empty bytes as padding between fields to ensure that each field satisfies its alignment requirements"* — that makes [[StructLayout|struct layout]] declaration-order-dependent. **74th ingested DIS chapter — ninth leaf of Ch 7.** Mints 4 new concept pages ([[StructLayout]], [[StructPadding]], [[AlignmentRule]], [[MemoryAlignment]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 7.4 Conditional Control and Loops (x86-64)](sources/dis-7-4-x86-64-conditional-loops.md) — **Fourth leaf** of Ch 7 *x86-64 Assembly* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* and the **hub page** opening the three-subsection treatment of [[ControlFlow|control flow]] at the [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] level. Follows [[dis-7-3-x86-64-arithmetic|Ch 7.3]]'s extended-arithmetic / bit-shift / bitwise / [[LeaInstruction|`lea`]] surface and pivots from **straight-line code** to **branch-driven non-sequential execution** — how the compiler translates [[CLanguage|C]]'s [[IfStatement|`if` / `else`]] and [[WhileLoop|`while`]] / [[ForLoop|`for`]] / [[DoWhileLoop|`do`–`while`]] constructs into instructions that **modify the [[InstructionPointer|`%rip`]] instruction pointer** based on evaluated conditions (*"modify the instruction pointer to alter program flow based on evaluated conditions"*). Three subsections (7.4.1 Preliminaries / 7.4.2 If Statements / 7.4.3 Loops) deliver the leaf mechanisms; this hub is intentionally short. **66th ingested DIS chapter — fourth leaf of Ch 7.** Hub-only — no new concept pages; subsection ingests will mint the condition-code / conditional-jump / branch-pattern pages.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 7.3 Additional Arithmetic Instructions (x86-64)](sources/dis-7-3-x86-64-arithmetic.md) — **Third leaf** of Ch 7 *x86-64 Assembly* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]*, following [[dis-7-2-x86-64-common|Ch 7.2]]'s data-movement / stack / `add`-`sub` primitives. **Expands the [[X86_64|x86-64]] arithmetic surface** with three new instruction families — **extended integer arithmetic** ([[X86NegInstruction|`neg`]] / `inc` / `dec`, [[X86MulInstruction|`imul`]], [[X86DivInstruction|`idiv`]]), **[[X86ShiftInstructions|bit-shift instructions]]** (`shl` / `sal` / `shr` / `sar`), and **[[X86BitwiseInstructions|bitwise logic instructions]]** (`and` / `or` / `xor` / `not`) — plus the **[[LeaInstruction|`lea` (load effective address)]] instruction**, the [[dis-7-2-x86-64-common|Ch 7.2]] forward-reference now delivered. Two headline pedagogical points: the `idiv` / multi-bit-shift hidden-operand conventions (*"prior to the execution of the `idiv` instruction, it is assumed that register `%rax` contains the dividend"*; *"the shift value `v` must either be a constant or stored in register `%cl`"*), and `lea` as an **address-arithmetic instruction that performs no memory access** (*"the `lea` instruction performs the same (sometimes complicated) operand arithmetic without the memory lookup"*) — exploited by compilers as a multi-operation arithmetic shortcut. The headline `not`-vs-`neg` clarification (*"the `not` instruction flips the bits but does not add 1"*) pins the `~x = -x - 1` identity to the assembly-instruction surface. The headline [[CompilerOptimization|strength-reduction]] quote — *"to compute `77 * 4`, most compilers will translate this operation to `77 << 2` to avoid the use of an `imul` instruction"* — surfaces the *shift-as-multiply* compiler pattern. **65th ingested DIS chapter — third leaf of Ch 7.** Mints 6 new concept pages ([[X86MulInstruction]], [[X86DivInstruction]], [[X86NegInstruction]], [[X86ShiftInstructions]], [[X86BitwiseInstructions]], [[LeaInstruction]] — last one promoted from forward-reference).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 7.2 Common Instructions (x86-64)](sources/dis-7-2-x86-64-common.md) — **Second leaf** of Ch 7 *x86-64 Assembly* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]*, following [[dis-7-1-x86-64-basics|Ch 7.1]]'s register / operand / addressing-mode framing. Introduces the **five most common [[X86_64|x86-64]] instructions** every assembly reader meets on sight: the data-movement primitive [[X86MovInstruction|`mov S, D`]] (*"copies a source value into a destination"*), the [[X86ArithmeticInstructions|arithmetic pair `add` / `sub`]] (`D ← D + S` and `D ← D − S` — the source-first AT&T order makes `sub` counterintuitive), and the [[X86StackInstructions|stack-management pair `push` / `pop`]] (specialized [[X86MovInstruction|`mov`]] + `sub`/`add` against [[StackPointer|`%rsp`]] — stack-grows-down, 8-byte step). Closes with a **step-by-step trace of [[dis-7-1-x86-64-basics|Ch 7.1]]'s `adder2` function** showing how the five instructions compose into a complete prologue / body / epilogue with [[CallStack|call-stack]] state tracked at each step — every `push` paired with a `pop`, the stack restored to entry state before `retq`. **Scope note**: the [[LeaInstruction|`lea`]] instruction is **not** covered here despite being commonly grouped with these primitives — it appears in a later Ch 7 section. **64th ingested DIS chapter — second leaf of Ch 7.** Mints 3 new concept pages ([[X86MovInstruction]], [[X86ArithmeticInstructions]], [[X86StackInstructions]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 7.1 Diving into Assembly: Basics (x86-64)](sources/dis-7-1-x86-64-basics.md) — **First ISA-specific section** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Part III, opening Ch 7 *x86-64 Assembly*. Walks `adder2` from C to [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] in [[AtAndTSyntax|AT&T syntax]] and supplies the wiki's canonical references for: the **16 [[GeneralPurposeRegister|GPRs]]** (`%rax`–`%rdx`, `%rdi`, `%rsi`, `%r8`–`%r15`) plus the three special-purpose `%rsp` / `%rbp` / `%rip`; the **subregister naming scheme** (`%rax` → `%eax` → `%ax` → `%al`/`%ah`; `%r8` → `%r8d` → `%r8w` → `%r8b`); the **System V calling convention** — *"the first six parameters in registers `%rdi`, `%rsi`, `%rdx`, `%rcx`, `%r8` and `%r9`"* with `%rax` as the return value; the **instruction-structure rule** opcode + source-then-destination operands; the **three [[Operand|operand types]]** (constant / register / memory) and the two structural constraints (no constant destinations, ≤ one memory operand per instruction); the **six [[X86AddressingMode|memory addressing modes]]** of `disp(base, index, scale)` with `scale ∈ {1,2,4,8}`; and the **[[OperandSize|size-suffix]] table** (`b`/`w`/`l`/`s`/`q`/`d` → 1/2/4/4/8/8 bytes). **63rd ingested DIS chapter — first ISA-specific section after Ch 6 hub.** Promotes [[X86_64]] from forward-ref stub to first-class [[ISA]] page; mints 6 new concept pages ([[X86_64]], [[GeneralPurposeRegister]], [[AtAndTSyntax]], [[IntelSyntax]], [[OperandSize]], [[Operand]], [[X86AddressingMode]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 6 Under the C: Diving into Assembly](sources/dis-6-asm-intro.md) — **Opens Part III *Assembly Programming*** of [[DiveIntoSystems]]. Single-page hub framing the three [[ISA]]-specific chapters that follow — Ch 7 [[X86_64|x86-64]], Ch 8 [[IA32]], Ch 9 [[ARM|ARMv8-A]]. Re-introduces [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] as *"the closest a programmer gets to coding at the machine level"* — the human-readable form of [[MachineCode|machine code]] — and motivates three chapters of ISA-specific detail via **four use cases**: (1) demystify what high-level code actually does at runtime, (2) embedded / resource-constrained programming, (3) security / vulnerability analysis, (4) performance-critical system code. Names the **four-category partition** every [[InstructionSet|ISA]] implements — arithmetic/logic, control flow, data movement, stack operations — as the structural unifier across the three dialects that follow. **62nd ingested DIS chapter — opens Part III after Ch 5 *Computer Architecture* closed at chapter 61.** Hub-only — no new concept pages, reuses [[AssemblyLanguage]] / [[MachineCode]] / [[InstructionSet]] / [[ISA]] / [[X86_64]] / [[IA32]] / [[ARM]].
- [DSPy Learn — Optimizers](sources/dspy-optimizers.md) — **Page 13 of 13** of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation and the **closing page of the corpus**. Where [[dspy-optimization-overview|the Optimization Overview]] (page 12) shipped the **workflow-level** contract (three inputs — *program + metric + training set*; one output — *optimized program*; 30/300 sizing; inverted 20/80 train/val split; four iteration axes), **this page ships the catalog** — the concrete `dspy.<OptimizerName>` registry enumerates: `LabeledFewShot` / [[BootstrapFewShot|`BootstrapFewShot`]] / [[BootstrapFewShotWithRandomSearch|`BootstrapFewShotWithRandomSearch`]] / `KNNFewShot` / `COPRO` / [[MIPROv2|`MIPROv2`]] / `SIMBA` / [[GEPA|`GEPA`]] / [[BootstrapFinetune|`BootstrapFinetune`]] / `Ensemble` / `BetterTogether`, grouped into five families (Automatic Few-Shot Learning / Automatic Instruction Optimization / Automatic Finetuning / Program Transformations / Meta-Optimizers). Names the historical rename — *"Formerly called teleprompters. We are making an official name update."* Reveals the **composability** claim: optimizers can be chained (`dspy.MIPROv2` then `dspy.BootstrapFinetune`, then top-k extraction into `dspy.Ensemble`) — the **structural essence** of `dspy.BetterTogether`. Three orthogonal what's-being-tuned axes: **demonstrations** (few-shot examples) / **instructions** (natural-language task descriptions) / **LM weights** (fine-tuning); only [[MIPROv2]] tunes more than one axis; only [[BootstrapFinetune]] tunes weights. Five-rule getting-started rubric: **10 examples → [[BootstrapFewShot]]**, **50+ → [[BootstrapFewShotWithRandomSearch]]**, **0-shot prompts → [[MIPROv2]] (0-shot mode)**, **40+ trials + 200+ examples → [[MIPROv2]] (full)**, **post-success efficiency → [[BootstrapFinetune]]**. Documents the **three-stage MIPROv2 algorithm** as the structural template for non-trivial optimizers: bootstrapping → grounded proposal → discrete search via [[BayesianOptimization|Bayesian Optimization]]. Records explicit operating-cost ballpark: *"A typical simple optimization run costs on the order of $2 USD and takes around ten minutes"*; *"a few cents up to tens of dollars"*. Three worked end-to-end receipts: **ReAct + MIPROv2(auto="light") on HotPotQA (24% → 51%)**, **RAG + MIPROv2(auto="medium") with [[llmasjudge|`SemanticF1`]] metric on StackExchange (53% → 61%)**, **Banking77 classification + BootstrapFinetune on `gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18` (66% → 87%, only weight-tuning receipt; 2000 examples; `Literal[tuple(CLASSES)]`-typed [[DSPySignatures|Signature]]; the only `set_lm(...)` exercise in the corpus)**. **Save/load inspectability**: `optimized_program.save(path)` produces plain-text JSON — consistent with DSPy's *"writing code instead of strings"* discipline. **Closes the DSPy *Learn* corpus at 13/13**; **resolves every long-standing forward reference** prior twelve pages carried — [[DSPyOptimizers]], [[BootstrapFewShot]], [[BootstrapFewShotWithRandomSearch]], [[MIPROv2]], [[BootstrapFinetune]], [[GEPA]] (the only optimizer named on page 12 as carve-out from the 20/80 split). Mints 6 concept pages — [[DSPyOptimizers]] (canonical catalog page, sibling to [[DSPyOptimization]] — workflow vs catalog, mirroring [[DSPyEvaluation]] / [[DSPyMetrics]]), [[BootstrapFewShot]], [[BootstrapFewShotWithRandomSearch]], [[MIPROv2]], [[GEPA]], [[BootstrapFinetune]]; folds minor variants (`KNNFewShot` / `COPRO` / `SIMBA` / `Ensemble` / `BetterTogether` / `LabeledFewShot`) into the catalog table on [[DSPyOptimizers]].
- [DSPy Learn — Optimization Overview](sources/dspy-optimization-overview.md) — **Page 12 of 13** of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation and the **opening page of the Optimization stage** in the [[dspy-learn-index|three-stage Programming → Evaluation → Optimization]] model. Where the Programming stage (pages 2–8) defined *how to express* a DSPy program and the Evaluation stage (pages 9–11) defined *how to measure* one, **this page defines *how to improve* one**. The canonical one-sentence definition: *"Once you have a system and a way to evaluate it, you can use DSPy optimizers to tune the prompts or weights in your program."* The page commits the framework to four load-bearing positions: (1) **the optimizer's three inputs are a program, a metric, and a training set** — DSPy's structural answer to *"what does it mean to optimize an LLM pipeline?"*; the output is an **optimized program** (same `dspy.Module` subclass, refined instructions / demonstrations / weights); (2) **training-set size scales from 30 to 300+** — *"You can often get substantial value out of 30 examples, but aim for at least 300 examples"* — an explicit expansion from [[DSPyEvaluation|the Evaluation stage's]] 20–200-example dev set, mirroring the *"start simple, then grow"* discipline at the training-set layer; (3) **the conventional ML train/val split is inverted to 20/80 for most prompt optimizers** — *"For most prompt optimizers, we recommend allocating 20% of your data for training and 80% for validation, contrary to typical deep learning conventions. This is because prompt optimizers tend to overfit on small training sets"* — with the **named exception of [[GEPA]]**, *"the only specific optimizer mentioned on this page"*, which *"follows standard ML practice — maximizing the training set size while keeping the validation set sufficiently sized to represent the downstream task distribution"*; (4) **iterative development spans four axes, not just optimizer-choice** — *"Iterative development is key. DSPy gives you the pieces to do that incrementally"* — across **data, program structure, metric, and optimizer**; three of the six diagnostic questions point **back into the Programming and Evaluation stages**, making the Optimization stage **open under revision from the prior two** (not a black-box terminus). Mints 1 concept page ([[DSPyOptimization]]) — the canonical anchor for the optimization **workflow** (the *fourth artifact* of [[DSPyProgrammingModel|the Programming Model]] — completes the four-artifact picture Signatures / Modules / Adapters / Optimizers at the workflow level alongside [[DSPyEvaluation|Evaluation]] as the connective stage between Programming and Optimization). Deliberately defers the **catalog** of specific optimizers ([[BootstrapFewShot]], [[BootstrapFewShotWithRandomSearch]], [[MIPROv2]], [[BootstrapFinetune]], [[GEPA]], and others) to page 13 ([[DSPyOptimizers|Optimizers]]) — the split mirrors the [[DSPyEvaluation]] / [[DSPyMetrics]] precedent of one page anchoring the workflow and the sibling page anchoring the per-algorithm machinery. The wiki's coverage of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* corpus is now 12/13; the single remaining sibling ingest ([[DSPyOptimizers|Optimizers]], page 13) will fill in the optimizer registry and resolve the [[DSPyOptimizers]] / [[BootstrapFewShot]] / [[BootstrapFewShotWithRandomSearch]] / [[MIPROv2]] / [[BootstrapFinetune]] / [[GEPA]] forward references this page carries.
- [DSPy Learn — Metrics](sources/dspy-metrics.md) — **Page 11 of 13** of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation; **third page of the [[DSPyEvaluation|Evaluation stage]]** (after [[dspy-evaluation-overview|the Evaluation Overview]] page 9 and [[dspy-data|Data Handling]] page 10). Expands **Step 2** of the four-step iterative-evaluation loop — *"define a DSPy metric"* — into the concrete **`(example, pred, trace=None) -> score`** function-signature contract every DSPy artifact composes against. Canonical claim: *"A DSPy metric is just a function in Python that takes `example` (e.g., from your training or dev set) and the output `pred` from your DSPy program, and outputs a `float` (or `int` or `bool`) score."* The page sharpens [[dspy-evaluation-overview|the Evaluation Overview's]] *"a function that takes examples from your data and takes the output of your system, and returns a score"* into a **typed Python function signature** with three structurally important properties: (a) **type-symmetric on the data side** — because [[DSPyPrediction|`dspy.Prediction`]] is a subclass of [[DSPyExample|`dspy.Example`]] ([[dspy-data|page 10]]), the metric author writes `example.answer == pred.answer` with no class-aware branching; (b) **regime-asymmetric on the calling side** — the optional third argument `trace` switches behavior between **evaluation/optimization** (`trace is None`, returns continuous `float`/`int`) and **bootstrapping** (`trace is not None`, returns strict `bool` for demo selection); (c) **scalar return** — `float` / `int` / `bool` are the only valid return types. Two regimes the Overview only named: **simple metrics** (one-line scalar comparisons — `example.answer.lower() == pred.answer.lower()`; built-ins `dspy.evaluate.metrics.answer_exact_match` and `dspy.evaluate.metrics.answer_passage_match`) for short-form tasks, and **AI-feedback metrics** (a `class Assess(dspy.Signature)` rubric template plus N `dspy.Predict(Assess)` invocations summed and thresholded) for long-form tasks — DSPy's structural operationalization of the [[llmasjudge|LLM-as-judge]] pattern. The tweet metric receipt is the canonical hybrid pattern: **multi-property AI judgment** (two `Predict(Assess)` calls) + **deterministic hard gate** (`len(tweet) <= 280`) + **regime-dependent return type** (`score >= 2` for bootstrap, `score / 2.0` for evaluation) — the wiki's first explicit demonstration that a DSPy metric is **not all-or-nothing AI-feedback**; it mixes LLM-as-judge with deterministic gates. Documents the **trace-aware bootstrap recipe** `validate_hops` — the only intermediate-step validator in the *Learn* corpus so far, inspecting `[outputs.query for *_, outputs in trace if 'query' in outputs]` to filter degenerate multi-hop trajectories at bootstrap-time. Operationalizes the **recursive-metric-optimization** claim ([[DSPyEvaluation|Step 4]] of the four-step loop) — the AI-feedback metric is itself a DSPy program (calls `dspy.Predict(Assess)`) and therefore is **optimizable by a [[DSPyOptimizers|DSPy Optimizer]]** the same way the system program is. Closes with **`dspy.Evaluate`** — the parallel dev-set-evaluation harness — documented via the four-kwarg construction signature (`devset` / `num_threads` / `display_progress` / `display_table`) and the **reusable two-phase pattern** (construct once with the dev set; call multiple times with `(program, metric)` pairs). Mints 2 concept pages — [[DSPyMetrics]] (the canonical `(example, pred, trace) -> score` contract; **resolves the long-standing forward reference** carried by [[DSPyEvaluation]] / [[dspy-evaluation-overview]] / [[dspy-data]] / [[DSPyExample]] / [[DSPyPrediction]] / every prior DSPy ingest) and [[DSPyEvaluate]] (the dev-set-evaluation utility — a thread-parallel wrapper around the raw `for x in devset: pred = program(**x.inputs()); score = metric(x, pred)` loop with progress + tabular display). Two sibling ingests remain to close the *Learn* corpus at 13/13: page 12 (Optimization Overview), page 13 ([[DSPyOptimizers|Optimizers]]).
- [DSPy Learn — Data Handling](sources/dspy-data.md) — **Page 10 of 13** of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation; **second page of the [[DSPyEvaluation|Evaluation stage]]** (after [[dspy-evaluation-overview|the Evaluation Overview]]). Expands **Step 1** of the four-step iterative-evaluation loop — *"collect an initial development set"* — into the concrete **data container** every other DSPy artifact reads from. Canonical claim: DSPy's data primitive is a typed Python dict-with-utilities — [[DSPyExample|`dspy.Example`]] — that (a) accepts arbitrary field names and value types (*"Examples can have any field keys and any value types, though usually values are strings"*), (b) carries an **input/label separation** as attached `input_keys` metadata rather than a structural partition (the `with_inputs("field1", ...)` method tags inputs; `inputs()` / `labels()` return non-mutating partition views), and (c) is the **parent class** that [[DSPyPrediction|`dspy.Prediction`]] subclasses (*"Your DSPy modules will return values of the type `Prediction`, which is a special sub-class of `Example`"*) — making the [[DSPyMetrics|metric]]'s `(example, prediction) -> score` contract type-symmetric. The page commits the framework to three load-bearing positions: (1) *"DSPy is a machine learning framework, so working in it involves training sets, development sets, and test sets"* — locates DSPy inside the supervised-ML tradition rather than presenting it as a separate paradigm; (2) **datasets are plain Python lists** of `dspy.Example` (*"trainset = [dspy.Example(report=..., summary=...), ...]"*) — DSPy does **not** introduce a `Dataset` class, a `train_test_split(...)` helper, or HuggingFace / CSV / JSON loaders; train/dev/test splits are Python slicing; (3) **inputs-only sufficiency** — *"You can use DSPy effectively without any intermediate or final labels, but you will need at least a few example inputs"* — the data-side mirror of [[dspy-evaluation-overview|the Evaluation Overview's]] *intermediate-step labels are almost never needed* commitment. The compact API surface — `dspy.Example(**fields)` construction, dot-notation access, `with_inputs(...)` tagging, `inputs()` / `labels()` partition accessors — is deliberately small; the framework reuses Python's `list` and `dict` semantics for everything that does not need framework-level machinery. Mints 2 concept pages — [[DSPyExample]] (the data primitive) and [[DSPyData]] (the dataset / split convention) — and **resolves both long-standing forward references** carried by [[DSPyEvaluation]] / [[dspy-evaluation-overview]] since the Evaluation stage opened on page 9.
- [DSPy Learn — Evaluation Overview](sources/dspy-evaluation-overview.md) — **Page 9 of 13** of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation and the **opening page of the Evaluation stage** in the [[dspy-learn-index|three-stage Programming → Evaluation → Optimization]] model. Operationalizes the Evaluation stage as a **four-step iterative loop**: (1) collect an initial development set of 20–200 examples — *"Even 20 input examples of your task can be useful, though 200 goes a long way"* — from adjacent public datasets ([[HuggingFace]] / StackExchange) → permissive-license re-use → manual labeling → deployed-demo collection; (2) define a DSPy metric as a callable `(example, prediction) -> score` — scalar `accuracy` for simple tasks, a **smaller DSPy program** for long-form tasks (DSPy's structural operationalization of the [[llmasjudge|LLM-as-judge]] pattern); (3) run development evaluations to produce a **baseline score** + a **qualitative diagnostic** that may force a return to the Programming stage rather than proceed forward; (4) (recursive) optimize the metric itself when it is a DSPy program — *"That's usually easy because the output of the metric is usually a simple value (e.g., a score out of 5), so the metric's metric is easy to define and optimize by collecting a few examples"*. Three load-bearing commitments distinguish DSPy Evaluation from generic ML evaluation: **small dev sets are sufficient** (20-example floor; 200-example ceiling for diminishing returns); **intermediate-step labels are almost never needed** — *"You almost never need labels for the intermediate steps in your program in DSPy"* — DSPy's structural answer to the intermediate-supervision problem in chain-of-thought training; **the metric is itself iterative** — *"Invest in defining metrics and improving them incrementally over time"* — the [[DSPyProgrammingModel|"start simple, then grow"]] discipline from page 2 restated at the metric layer. Mints 1 concept page ([[DSPyEvaluation]]) as the canonical anchor for DSPy's evaluation philosophy. Motivates the next two pages — **Data Handling** (page 10, forward reference [[DSPyData]]) which will expand Step 1 into [[DSPyExample|`dspy.Example`]] mechanics, and **[[DSPyMetrics|Metrics]]** (page 11, forward reference) which will expand Step 2 into the full `(example, prediction) -> score` contract — without overstepping into either; the deliberate scope limit lets sibling ingests fill in the data-handling and metric machinery.
- [DSPy Learn — MCP](sources/dspy-mcp.md) — **Page 8 of 13** of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation. Defines DSPy's integration with the **[[ModelContextProtocol|Model Context Protocol (MCP)]]** — [[anthropic|Anthropic]]'s open protocol that standardizes how applications expose tools, resources, and context to language models. **DSPy does not manage MCP server connections directly**; the user opens a `ClientSession` via the `mcp` Python SDK and uses **[[DSPyMCP|`dspy.Tool.from_mcp_tool(session, tool)`]]** to convert each MCP-side tool descriptor into a [[DSPyTools|`dspy.Tool`]] instance. Converted tools then compose through every existing DSPy pathway — [[react|`dspy.ReAct`]] as the canonical entry point — without any further MCP-aware code. Two transports: **stdio** (`stdio_client` + `StdioServerParameters` for local processes) and **streamable HTTP** (`streamablehttp_client` for remote servers). Both share the same `ClientSession` API once open — the conversion code is byte-identical across transports. **MCP execution is asynchronous end-to-end**: [[react|`dspy.ReAct`]] must be invoked via `.acall(...)` and the agent invocation must live inside the `async with` session block (the session closes when the block exits; further tool calls would fail). Installation: `pip install -U "dspy[mcp]"`. Mints 2 concept pages — [[ModelContextProtocol]] (the framework-agnostic protocol; **resolves the long-standing forward reference** carried by [[DSPy]] / [[DSPyTools]] / [[dspy-learn-index]] / [[dspy-tools]]) and [[DSPyMCP]] (the DSPy-specific binding, lighter-weight; the split mirrors the [[LiteLLM]] / [[DSPyLM]] precedent of protocol/library upstream + framework-binding downstream). Updates [[anthropic|Anthropic]] entity page in-place with MCP-authorship attribution — a new wiki role for Anthropic alongside its frontier-model and managed-API-provider roles. **First external tool-source protocol the corpus records** — confirms the [[DSPyTools|`dspy.Tool`]] abstraction is open under tool origin (local function vs MCP server) and vindicates the [[dspy-tools|page-7]] async-tool surface (`tool.acall(...)`, `dspy.context(allow_tool_async_sync_conversion=True)`) as load-bearing infrastructure rather than corner-case feature.
- [DSPy Learn — Tools](sources/dspy-tools.md) — Page 7 of 13 of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation. Defines the **Tools** sub-system — the primitive DSPy uses to let an [[DSPyLM|LM]] invoke external Python functions. Presents **two equal-status approaches**: **(1)** the **fully-managed** [[react|`dspy.ReAct`]] [[DSPyModules|Module]] (framework-owned think-act-observe loop; the returned [[DSPyPrediction|`Prediction`]] carries a `trajectory` field tracking every reasoning step and tool call) and **(2)** **manual handling** via [[DSPyPredict|`dspy.Predict`]] over a [[DSPySignatures|Signature]] whose input is `tools: list[dspy.Tool]` and whose output is `dspy.ToolCalls` (user owns the loop). Documents the [[DSPyTools|`dspy.Tool`]] wrapper surface — `.name` (from `__name__`), `.desc` (from docstring), `.args` (from type hints + defaults), `str(tool)` (the canonical text the LM sees) — plus the `dspy.ToolCalls` model-output type and the three `ToolCall.execute()` lookup modes (automatic-by-name / `functions={}` dict / `functions=[]` `Tool` list — **requires DSPy 3.0.4b2+**). **Native function calling** is configured at the [[DSPyAdapters|Adapter]] layer via `use_native_function_calling=` (defaults: [[DSPyAdapters|`ChatAdapter`]]=`False`, [[DSPyAdapters|`JSONAdapter`]]=`True`; automatic fallback to text-based parsing for models that don't support it — the **second model-capability scoping** in the [[dspy-learn-index|Learn corpus]] after [[DSPyAdapters|`JSONAdapter`]]'s `response_format` requirement). **Async tools** are first-class via `tool.acall(...)` plus the `dspy.context(allow_tool_async_sync_conversion=True)` sync-from-async opt-in. Three tool-function design rules: clear, detailed docstrings; explicit type hints; prefer basic types or [[Pydantic|Pydantic]] models. Names *void-return tools* as the most informative reason to choose manual handling (managed [[react|`dspy.ReAct`]]'s loop feeds observations back into reasoning, so side-effect-only tools — logging, telemetry, fire-and-forget actions — don't fit). Mints 1 concept page ([[DSPyTools]]) — **resolves the long-standing forward reference** carried by [[DSPy]] / [[DSPyProgrammingModel]] / [[DSPySignatures]] / [[DSPyLM]] / [[DSPyModules]] / [[DSPyAdapters]] / [[react|ReAct]] / [[dspy-learn-index]] / [[dspy-programming-overview]] / [[dspy-language-models]] / [[dspy-signatures]] / [[dspy-modules]] / [[dspy-adapters]] since the corpus opened on 2026-05-17. Extends [[react|ReAct]] in-place with a *managed-vs-manual* duality section rather than minting a parallel `DSPyReAct` page.
- [DSPy Learn — Adapters](sources/dspy-adapters.md) — Page 6 of 13 of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation. **Defines** the **third** of the four orthogonal artifacts [[DSPyProgrammingModel|the Programming Model]] factors out of a conventional prompt — the **Adapter**: *"the bridge between `dspy.Predict` and the actual Language Model (LM)"*. Three responsibilities: (1) convert a [[DSPySignatures|Signature]] into a system message; (2) format input data (multi-turn messages, demo injection, conversation history, function calls, and DSPy-special types — [[DSPyTools|`Tool`]] / `dspy.Image` / `dspy.History`) into the LM's request shape; (3) parse the LM's textual response into a typed [[DSPyPrediction|`dspy.Prediction`]]. Two configuration channels — `dspy.configure(adapter=...)` (global) and `with dspy.context(adapter=...)` (block-local) — mirror the [[DSPyLM|LM]] bind modes. Two introspection hooks: `adapter.format(signature, demos, inputs)` returns the full multi-turn message list; `adapter.format_system_message(signature)` returns only the system message. Documents two built-in adapters in detail: **`dspy.ChatAdapter`** (the default; uses `[[ ## field_name ## ]]` delimiters; inlines JSON schemas for non-primitive types; *"universal compatibility: works with all language models"*; includes **automatic fallback to `JSONAdapter` on failure**; trade-off — *"more boilerplate output tokens compared to other adapters"*) and **`dspy.JSONAdapter`** (uses the LM's native `response_format` parameter — *"effective for models that support structured output"*; minimal boilerplate → lower latency; **model-capability-gated** — *"requires models supporting the `response_format` parameter; incompatible with smaller open-source models lacking this capability"* — the **first explicit model-capability boundary** in the [[dspy-learn-index|Learn corpus]]). Two further built-ins named only — **`dspy.XMLAdapter`** (XML-formatted I/O) and **`dspy.TwoStepAdapter`** (two-step extract-then-format workflow). Custom adapters supported via `Adapter`-subclass + `format()`/`parse()` override. Worked example: the same `NewsQA` [[DSPySignatures|Signature]] with a `list[pydantic.BaseModel]` output runs under both adapters with a **one-kwarg edit** — the page's most explicit *"swap the adapter without touching the signature"* demonstration, the third concrete *"swap N, leave M unchanged"* receipt in the wiki after [[DSPyLM|`dspy.LM`]]'s LM-swap and [[DSPyModules|`dspy.Module`]]'s strategy-swap. Mints 1 concept page ([[DSPyAdapters]]) — **resolves the long-standing forward reference** carried by [[DSPy]] / [[DSPyProgrammingModel]] / [[DSPySignatures]] / [[DSPyLM]] / [[DSPyModules]] / [[dspy-learn-index]] / [[dspy-programming-overview]] / [[dspy-language-models]] / [[dspy-signatures]] / [[dspy-modules]] since the corpus opened on 2026-05-17.
- [DSPy Learn — Modules](sources/dspy-modules.md) — Page 5 of 13 of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation. **Defines** the second of the four orthogonal artifacts [[DSPyProgrammingModel|the Programming Model]] factors out of a conventional prompt — the **Module**: *"a building block for programs that use LMs"*, where *"each built-in module abstracts a prompting technique"* and the same module is *"generalized to handle any signature."* Establishes [[DSPyPredict|`dspy.Predict`]] as the **minimal primitive every other Module is built on top of** (*"Internally, all other DSPy modules are built using `dspy.Predict`"*) and enumerates the seven built-ins: [[DSPyPredict|`dspy.Predict`]] (identity — *"does not modify the signature"*; stores instructions + demonstrations + LM-weight updates), [[ChainOfThought|`dspy.ChainOfThought`]] (*"teaches the LM to think step-by-step"* — adds a `reasoning` field to the user's signature under the hood; *"in many cases, simply swapping `dspy.ChainOfThought` in place of `dspy.Predict` improves quality"*), [[DSPyProgramOfThought|`dspy.ProgramOfThought`]] (*"teaches the LM to output code, whose execution results will dictate the response"*), [[react|`dspy.ReAct`]] (tool-using agent; `tools=[...]` kwarg of plain Python callables), [[DSPyMultiChainComparison|`dspy.MultiChainComparison`]] (N CoT samples + LM comparison Predict), [[DSPyRecursiveLanguageModel|`dspy.RLM`]] (**Recursive Language Model** — sandboxed Python REPL + recursive sub-LLM calls *"when context is too large to fit in the prompt effectively"*), and function-style [[DSPyMajority|`dspy.majority`]] (vote over a set of [[DSPyPrediction|`Prediction`]]s; **zero LM cost**). Composes via `class MyProgram(dspy.Module)` with PyTorch-shaped `__init__` (sub-modules as `self.*` attributes for `named_predictors()` / `named_parameters()` walks that [[DSPyOptimizers|Optimizers]] consume) and `forward(...)`; *"DSPy is just Python code that uses modules in any control flow you like, with a little magic internally at compile time to trace your LM calls."* Documents the LM-usage telemetry surface (DSPy 2.6.16+): `dspy.configure(track_usage=True)` plus `prediction.get_lm_usage()` returning `{provider/model: {prompt/completion/total tokens + details}}` aggregated across every LM call inside `forward()`, with cached responses correctly returning `{}` per [[LiteLLM]]'s cache discipline. Five worked examples (math / RAG / classification with `Literal[...]` / information extraction / ReAct agent) plus the canonical multi-hop search `class Hop(dspy.Module)`. Mints 7 concept pages: [[DSPyModules]] (resolves the long-standing forward reference carried by [[DSPy]] / [[DSPyProgrammingModel]] / [[DSPySignatures]] / [[DSPyLM]] / [[dspy-learn-index]] / [[dspy-programming-overview]] / [[dspy-language-models]] / [[dspy-signatures]]), [[DSPyPredict]], [[DSPyProgramOfThought]], [[DSPyMultiChainComparison]], [[DSPyRecursiveLanguageModel]], [[DSPyMajority]], [[DSPyPrediction]]. Extends [[ChainOfThought]] and [[react|ReAct]] **in place** with *DSPy implementation* sections rather than minting `DSPyChainOfThought` / `DSPyReAct` duplicates.
- [DSPy Learn — Signatures](sources/dspy-signatures.md) — Page 4 of 13 of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation. **Defines** the first of the four orthogonal artifacts [[DSPyProgrammingModel|the Programming Model]] factors out of a conventional prompt — the **Signature**, *"a declarative specification of input/output behavior of a DSPy module"*. Documents both surface forms: **inline** strings like `"sentence -> sentiment: bool"`, `"context: list[str], question: str -> answer: str"` (RAG QA), `"question, choices: list[str] -> reasoning: str, selection: int"` (multi-output) — with an `instructions=` kwarg for top-level guidance; and **class-based** signatures (`class Emotion(dspy.Signature)`) which add three things the inline form cannot — task-description **docstring**, **`dspy.InputField(desc=...)`** input hints, and **`dspy.OutputField(desc=...)`** output constraints. Enumerates the five-tier type system: basic Python (`str` / `int` / `bool`), `typing` composites (`list[str]` / `dict[str, int]` / `Optional[float]` / `Union[str, int]`), arbitrary pydantic models, dot-notation nested types (`MyContainer.Query`), and DSPy-special types `dspy.Image` (multi-modal input via `dspy.Image.from_url(...)`) + `dspy.History` (conversational context). Names `typing.Literal[...]` as the DSPy-idiomatic closed-set classification primitive and demonstrates input-type-checking as warn-not-fail (`dspy.configure(warn_on_type_mismatch=False)` to disable). Most consequential implementation note: *"Many DSPy modules expand signatures under the hood. For example, `dspy.ChainOfThought` adds a `reasoning` field."* — the mechanism that lets a user's `'document -> summary'` Signature acquire a `response.reasoning` slot without the user declaring it. Closes with the framework's value claim: *"their primary value emerges when composing multiple signatures into larger DSPy modules and compiling these into optimized prompts and finetunings."* Mints 1 concept page ([[DSPySignatures]]) — resolves the long-standing forward reference carried by [[DSPy]] / [[DSPyProgrammingModel]] / [[DSPyLM]] / [[dspy-learn-index]] / [[dspy-programming-overview]] / [[dspy-language-models]] since the corpus opened on 2026-05-17.
- [DSPy Learn — Language Models](sources/dspy-language-models.md) — Page 3 of 13 of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation. Operationalizes [[dspy-programming-overview|the Programming Overview's]] *"swap the LM without changing the rest of your logic"* portability claim into a **two-line code change** via the [[DSPyLM|`dspy.LM`]] universal client — `provider/model-name` string + `dspy.configure(lm=...)` (global, thread-safe) or `with dspy.context(lm=...):` (block-local, thread-safe). Names **[[LiteLLM]]** as the upstream provider-abstraction layer DSPy routes through (*"DSPy supports dozens of LLM providers via LiteLLM"*) and demonstrates one API spanning three deployment regimes: **managed** ([[openai|OpenAI]] / [[anthropic|Anthropic]] / [[gemini|Gemini]] / Vertex AI / [[Databricks]] / [[Anyscale]] / [[TogetherAI|Together AI]] / [[microsoft|Azure]]), **self-hosted GPU** ([[SGLang]] via OpenAI-compatible endpoint), and **local laptop** ([[Ollama]]). Adds four framework-level capabilities on top of LiteLLM: default-on **caching** (`cache=False` to disable), **`rollout_id`** deterministic cache-busting (OpenAI / Databricks), per-call **`lm.history`** telemetry (`prompt / messages / kwargs / response / outputs / usage / cost / timestamp / uuid / model / response_model / model_type`), and **`model_type="responses"`** opt-in for [[openai|OpenAI]]'s Responses API. Mints 1 concept ([[DSPyLM]]) and 4 entities ([[LiteLLM]], [[Ollama]], [[SGLang]], [[TogetherAI]]).
- [DSPy Learn — Programming Overview](sources/dspy-programming-overview.md) — Page 2 of 13 of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation; opens the **Programming** stage of the [[dspy-learn-index|three-stage model]] and operationalizes it as **define your task → define your initial pipeline → craft a handful of examples**. Anchors DSPy's framework-level thesis — *"DSPy is a bet on writing code instead of strings"* — and names the **four concerns** a conventional prompt entangles into one non-portable string: **signature** (typed I/O), **adapter** (formatting / parsing), **module logic** (strategy, e.g. "thinking step by step"), and **manual optimization** (trial-and-error). DSPy *separates* these concerns and *automates* the lower-level ones, yielding three concrete portability claims: swap the LM/adapter without touching pipeline code; swap one module for another (`dspy.ChainOfThought` ↔ `dspy.ProgramOfThought`) without modifying [[DSPySignatures|signatures]]; run prompt-optimization *or* weight fine-tuning against the same program. Recommends starting simple — *"perhaps with just a single `dspy.ChainOfThought` module"* — and adding complexity incrementally. Mints one concept page ([[DSPyProgrammingModel]]) covering the separation-of-concerns philosophy.
- [DSPy Learn — Index](sources/dspy-learn-index.md) — Top-level index page of the [[DSPy]] *Learn* documentation. Frames DSPy as a small learnable API for building AI systems through a strict **three-stage development model**: **Programming** ("defining your task, its constraints, exploring a few examples, and using that to inform your initial pipeline design") → **Evaluation** ("collect an initial development set, define your DSPy metric, and use these to iterate on your system more systematically") → **Optimization** ("use DSPy optimizers to tune the prompts or weights in your program"). The stage order is load-bearing: *"it's unproductive to launch optimization runs using a poorly designed program or a bad metric."* Indexes 12 sub-pages — Programming Overview / Language Models / [[DSPySignatures|Signatures]] / [[DSPyModules|Modules]] / [[DSPyAdapters|Adapters]] / [[DSPyTools|Tools]] / [[ModelContextProtocol|MCP]] / Evaluation Overview / Data Handling / [[DSPyMetrics|Metrics]] / Optimization Overview / [[DSPyOptimizers|Optimizers]] — that will be filled in by sibling ingests. **Page 1 of 13** of the DSPy Learn corpus; opens the wiki's first dedicated LLM-programming-framework source cluster.

D$ — and avoids the [[AverageTrap]] (irreducible quadratic penalty from conflicting per-task gradients). General agentic systems formalized as DAGs $\Psi\!=\!(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{F},\Lambda)$ with [[CompositionalCapacity]] $C(\mathcal{G})$ and [[TopologicalEdgeWeight]] decomposition as principled design tools; [[MixtureOfExperts|MoE]] reinterpreted as the single-layer routing instance.

Pedagogical thesis: teach concepts *just-in-time*, interleaving *concepts / context / code*; "one working example, one notebook".
