- [Dive into Systems — Ch 5.2 The von Neumann Architecture](sources/dis-5-2-von-neumann.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **operational follow-up** to [[dis-5-1-history|Ch 5.1]]'s historical narrative — decomposes the [[VonNeumannArchitecture|von Neumann architecture]] into **five functional units** ([[ControlUnit|control unit]] + [[ProcessingUnit|processing unit]] = [[CPU]]; [[RAM|memory unit]]; [[InputDevice|input unit]]; [[OutputDevice|output unit]]) connected by three [[Bus|system buses]] ([[ControlBus|control]] / [[AddressBus|address]] / [[DataBus|data]]). [[ProcessingUnit|Processing unit]] = [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] + [[CpuRegister|register file]]; [[ControlUnit|control unit]] owns the [[ProgramCounter|PC]] and [[InstructionRegister|IR]]. Operational restatement of the [[StoredProgram|stored-program]] principle: *"there is no distinction between instructions and data in the von Neumann architecture"* — they share [[RAM|memory]] **and** [[CpuRegister|register]] storage. Architecture's *operational heart* is the **[[FetchDecodeExecuteCycle|fetch-decode-execute-store cycle]]**: fetch instruction at [[ProgramCounter|PC]] into [[InstructionRegister|IR]] → decode opcode + operand locations → [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] executes → store result via the buses → repeat. [[RAM|Memory]] is **[[ByteAddressable|byte-addressable]]** — a 32-bit [[AddressBus|address bus]] caps it at $2^{32}$ bytes (4 GiB). Touchscreens / storage drives / NICs are bidirectional [[IODevice|I/O devices]]. **15 new concept pages** ([[ControlUnit]], [[ArithmeticLogicUnit]], [[ProcessingUnit]], [[Bus]], [[ControlBus]], [[AddressBus]], [[DataBus]], [[IODevice]], [[InputDevice]], [[OutputDevice]], [[FetchDecodeExecuteCycle]], [[ProgramCounter]], [[InstructionRegister]], [[ByteAddressable]], [[DataWord]]) + 4 in-place expansions ([[VonNeumannArchitecture]] / [[CPU]] / [[CpuRegister]] / [[StoredProgram]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 5.1 The Origins of Modern Computing](sources/dis-5-1-history.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s opening section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 5 *Computer Architecture* — the corpus's first descent into **historical lineage** rather than a technical mechanism. Traces how the [[VonNeumannArchitecture|stored-program]] model emerged in the **1930s–1940s** as a **convergence** of independent threads: [[ClaudeShannon|Shannon]]'s [[BooleanAlgebra|Boolean]] circuit thesis (1937), [[AlanTuring|Turing]]'s [[TuringMachine|abstract machine]] (1937), [[KonradZuse|Zuse]]'s [[Z3]] (1941), [[TommyFlowers|Flowers]]'s [[Colossus]] (1943), [[HowardAiken|Aiken]]'s [[HarvardMarkI|Mark I]] (1944), [[JohnMauchly|Mauchly]] / [[PresperEckert|Eckert]]'s [[ENIAC]] (1945), and [[JohnVonNeumann|von Neumann]]'s [[EDVAC]] paper — **not a single linear progression**. Explicitly foregrounds the women whose contributions were historically underrecognized (the six [[ENIAC]] programmers; [[GraceHopper]]; the [[WomensRoyalNavalService|WRNS]] operators of [[Colossus]]). Closes by naming the [[VonNeumannArchitecture|von Neumann architecture]] — **instructions + data in the same internal memory** — as the unifying synthesis Ch 5.2+ operationalizes. **10 new entity pages** ([[AlanTuring]], [[JohnVonNeumann]], [[CharlesBabbage]], [[AdaLovelace]], [[KonradZuse]], [[TommyFlowers]], [[HowardAiken]], [[JohnMauchly]], [[PresperEckert]], [[GraceHopper]]); **9 new concept pages** ([[TuringMachine]], [[VonNeumannArchitecture]], [[Z3]], [[Colossus]], [[HarvardMarkI]], [[ENIAC]], [[EDVAC]], [[AnalyticalEngine]], [[StoredProgram]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 0 Introduction](sources/dis-0-introduction.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] ([[UnitedStatesMilitaryAcademy|West Point]]), [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] & [[KevinCWebb|Webb]] ([[SwarthmoreCollege]]) open *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* with the thesis that **understanding what a [[ComputerSystem|computer system]] is and how it runs your programs lets you write efficient code**. Defines a computer system as [[ComputerHardware|hardware]] ([[CPU]] / [[RAM]] / I/O / storage) **plus** an [[OperatingSystem|OS]] that delivers [[Abstraction|abstractions]], policies, and mechanisms — pointedly excluding calculators and bare [[Microcontroller|microcontrollers]] from the definition. Surveys modern form factors ([[SingleBoardComputer|SBCs]] like the [[RaspberryPi]], smartphone [[SystemOnAChip|SoCs]], universally [[MulticoreProcessor|multicore]]) and previews the book's C-centric, active-reading pedagogy across [[BinaryRepresentation|binary representation]], architecture, OS, [[MemoryHierarchy|memory hierarchy]], and [[ParallelComputing|multicore parallel programming]]. **Opens the *Dive into Systems* corpus**; complements the embedded-`no_std` world of [[TheEmbeddedRustBook]] from the **OS-yes** side of the [[HardwareAbstractionLayer|HAL]] split.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 1.1 Getting Started Programming in C](sources/dis-1-1-getting-started.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s first content section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 1 *By the C, the Beautiful C*. Cross-walks [[Python]] vs. [[CLanguage|C]] on the canonical hello-world: `#include` ≠ `import`, `{ }` blocks ≠ indentation, `;`-terminated statements, [[Printf|`printf`]] without auto-`\n`. Introduces the [[CompilationProcess|compile-then-run]] model with [[GCC|`gcc hello.c`]] / `./a.out` / `-o` / `-Wall` / `-g` / `-lm`, the [[MainFunction|`int main(void)`]] entry point and its [[ExitStatus|`return 0`]] success convention, the [[VariableDeclaration|`type_name variable_name;`]] *declare-before-use* rule, the [[CPrimitiveType|byte-width table]] for `char`/`short`/`int`/`long`/`long long`/`float`/`double` plus `unsigned` variants, the [[SizeOf|`sizeof`]] operator, the `'h'`-char-vs-`"h"`-string distinction, and the [[CArithmeticOperators|arithmetic operator]] set — flagging the [[IntegerDivision|integer-division truncation]] (`11/2 == 5`, `11/2.0 == 5.5`) and pre/post-[[IncrementOperator|`++`]] traps. **Delivers the minimum C-toolchain surface area** that [[dis-0-introduction|Ch 0]]'s *active-reading-by-typing-the-code* promise requires.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 1.2 Input/Output (printf and scanf)](sources/dis-1-2-input-output.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s second content section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 1. Formalizes hosted [[CLanguage|C]] I/O via the [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] pair [[Printf|`printf`]] / [[Scanf|`scanf`]]: the [[FormatSpecifier|`%`-specifier]] vocabulary (`%d` int, `%g` float/double, `%s` string, `%c` char), the matched-arity rule, [[EscapeSequence|`\n`-is-explicit]] (restated from [[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]]), and the same-`char`-two-displays trick (`%d` → `65`, `%c` → `A`). Introduces the [[AddressOfOperator|address-of operator `&`]] as the *first sighting of a [[CMemoryAddress|memory address]] as a value* — needed because [[Scanf|`scanf`]] must be told **where** to deposit each parsed value, not just **what type**. Covers `scanf`'s whitespace-skipping between numeric reads and its [[Scanf|fragility]] under malformed input (Ctrl-C escape; Ch 2 has the robust recipe). The Python-vs-C input contrast: `input()` returns `str` requiring conversion, `scanf` parses typed values directly into typed memory locations.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 1.3 Conditionals and Loops](sources/dis-1-3-conditionals-loops.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s third content section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 1. Adds the [[ControlFlow|control-flow]] layer on top of [[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]]'s types/arithmetic: [[IfStatement|`if`]] / [[ElseStatement|`else` / `else if`]] branching with parenthesized tests and `{ }` blocks (not Python-style indentation), the [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]] / [[CaseLabel|`case`]] integer-dispatch construct with its **fall-through-by-default** semantics requiring an explicit [[BreakStatement|`break`]], and the three loop forms [[WhileLoop|`while`]] (test-first, zero-or-more), [[DoWhileLoop|`do`–`while`]] (test-last, at-least-once, semicolon-terminated), and [[ForLoop|`for`]] (general three-clause `init; cond; step` loop, *not* sequence iteration as in [[Python]]). Codifies the **integer-as-boolean** rule ([[CBooleanExpression|`0` is false, any nonzero true]]), the [[RelationalOperator|`==` `!=` `<` `<=` `>` `>=`]] family (with the `=`-vs-`==` footgun), the [[LogicalOperator|`!` `&&` `||`]] family with [[ShortCircuitEvaluation|short-circuit evaluation]] making `if (p != NULL && *p == 0)` safe, the [[CommaOperator|comma operator]] for chaining init/step expressions, and the design rule **[[ForLoop|`for`]] for [[DefiniteIteration|definite]] iteration, [[WhileLoop|`while`]] for [[IndefiniteIteration|indefinite]] iteration** despite the two being capability-equivalent. [[BreakStatement|`break`]] exits the innermost loop or [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]]; [[ContinueStatement|`continue`]] skips to the next iteration (running [[ForLoop|`for`]]'s step first).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 1.7 Summary](sources/dis-1-7-summary.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s closing summary of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 1 *By the C, the Beautiful C*. Short recap (no new material): cross-walks [[Python]] vs [[CLanguage|C]] across [[VariableDeclaration|variables]] / [[ControlFlow|loops/conditionals]] / [[Function|functions]] / [[StandardIOLibrary|I/O]] and isolates two **headline differences** — (1) [[VariableDeclaration|declare-before-use typed variables]] (from [[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]]), (2) lower-level [[CArray|arrays]] and [[CString|strings]] vs. [[Python]] list/str (from [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]]). Pay-off: lower-level constructs give *"a C programmer more control over how their program accesses its memory and thus more control over their program's efficiency"* — restating [[dis-0-introduction|Ch 0]]'s thesis. Forward-references Ch 2 (*A Deeper Dive Into C*) for **pointer variables** and **dynamic memory allocation** — the two big language features Ch 1 deferred and on which [[ArrowOperator|`->`]] / [[Typedef|`typedef`]] / [[ArrayOfStructs|arrays of structs]] / [[Strcpy|`strcpy`]]-safety / robust [[Scanf|`scanf`]] all hinge. **Closes Ch 1 of the *Dive into Systems* corpus.**
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 1.8 Exercises](sources/dis-1-8-exercises.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s exercise set that closes *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 1 *By the C, the Beautiful C*. A single-page redirect (*"All Chapter 1 Exercises"*) into the book's interactive exercises platform rather than inline problems — drills the Ch 1.1–Ch 1.6 surface area: [[CompilationProcess|compile-then-run]] with [[GCC|`gcc`]], [[VariableDeclaration|typed declarations]] / [[CPrimitiveType|primitive types]] / [[CArithmeticOperators|arithmetic]] / [[IntegerDivision|integer-division traps]] ([[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]]); [[Printf|`printf`]] / [[Scanf|`scanf`]] [[FormatSpecifier|format specifiers]] and the [[AddressOfOperator|`&` address-of]] discipline ([[dis-1-2-input-output|Ch 1.2]]); [[IfStatement|`if`]] / [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]] / [[WhileLoop|`while`]] / [[DoWhileLoop|`do`-`while`]] / [[ForLoop|`for`]] [[ControlFlow|control-flow]] ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops|Ch 1.3]]); [[FunctionDefinition|function definitions]] / [[FunctionPrototype|prototypes]] / [[PassByValue|pass-by-value]] ([[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]); [[CArray|array]] indexing and [[CString|C-string]] / [[NullTerminator|null-terminator]] handling with [[StringLibrary|`<string.h>`]] ([[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]]); and [[CStruct|struct]] [[MemberAccessOperator|`.`-field-access]] / [[StructAssignment|whole-record copy]] ([[dis-1-6-structs|Ch 1.6]]). No new conceptual material — operationalizes [[dis-0-introduction|Ch 0]]'s *active-reading-by-typing-the-code* pedagogy. **Final section of Ch 1 — Ch 1 *By the C, the Beautiful C* is now fully complete.**
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.5 Overflow](sources/dis-4-5-overflow.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.5** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **detection-rules section** that formalizes the [[IntegerOverflow|integer-overflow]] phenomenon [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]] and [[dis-4-4-2-subtraction|Ch 4.4.2]] named-and-deferred. Defines overflow as *"a computation that lacks the storage to represent its result has **overflowed**"* and supplies the **two encoding-specific detection rules**: (1) **unsigned** — *"the carry out must match the carry in, otherwise the operation causes overflow"* (MSB [[CarryOut|carry-out]] in addition mode = overflow; absent expected carry-out in subtraction mode = overflow — resolving [[dis-4-4-2-subtraction|Ch 4.4.2]]'s deferred caveat); (2) **[[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] signed** — same-sign operands producing a different-sign result indicates overflow (mixed-sign addition can never overflow). Worked 4-bit examples: $4 + 5 = -7$ (pos + pos → neg = overflow); $-3 + (-8) = 5$ (neg + neg → pos = overflow); $5 + (-4) = 1$ (mixed → no overflow possible). The **same N-bit [[FullAdder|adder]]** produces both `CF` (unsigned) and `OF` (signed) flag signals simultaneously; software / the [[CCompiler|C compiler]] chooses which to consult based on operand types — the operational pay-off of [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4]]'s interpretation-invariance thesis. Three canonical real-world consequences cited: **YouTube view counter (2014)** approaching $2^{32}-1$ on Gangnam Style (migrated to 64-bit pre-wrap); **Pac-Man (1980)** 8-bit unsigned level counter wrapping at level $256$ (the *"split-screen kill screen"*); **[[Therac25|Therac-25]] (1980s)** flag-variable overflow *"bypassed safety mechanisms"* contributing to patient radiation overdoses. Chapter stays at hardware-mechanics layer — does **not** discuss the [[CLanguage|C]]-language semantics (signed overflow is [[UndefinedBehavior|UB]]; unsigned is defined wrap), captured separately on [[UndefinedBehavior]]. **Closes the deferral chain** from [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]] (*"the hardware simply drops or truncates"* the MSB carry-out — Ch 4.5 says what it *means*) and [[dis-4-4-2-subtraction|Ch 4.4.2]] (*"doesn't necessarily indicate overflow"* — Ch 4.5 supplies the full rule). **2 new concept pages** ([[IntegerOverflow]] — promoted from forward-reference stub; [[UndefinedBehavior]] — new). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **42 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.4.3 Multiplication and Division](sources/dis-4-4-3-mult-div.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.4.3** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **third and final subsection** of [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4 *Binary Integer Arithmetic*]]; **closes the [[BinaryArithmetic|binary integer arithmetic]] block**. Transfers the pencil-and-paper **long-multiplication** and **long-division** algorithms from decimal to base $2$, instantiating the [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4]] base-transfer thesis on the two remaining arithmetic operations. Opens with the explicit scope disclaimer *"these methods do not reflect the behavior of modern hardware and are not meant to be comprehensive"* — Ch 4.4.3 is deliberately a **manual-calculation** treatment, not a hardware-multiplier or hardware-divider treatment. **[[BinaryMultiplication|Multiplication]]**: per-multiplier-bit partial-product rows (each row is *the multiplicand itself or zero* — binary's digit alphabet $\{0,1\}$ eliminates decimal's $9\times 9$ multiplication table), each shifted left by its bit position, summed via [[BinaryAddition|Ch 4.4.1 binary addition]]; worked example $\mathtt{0b0101} \times \mathtt{0b0011}$ (5 × 3) → $\mathtt{0b0101} + \mathtt{0b1010} = \mathtt{0b1111}$ (15). **[[BinaryDivision|Division]]**: grade-school long division with the per-step "fits / doesn't fit" decision reducing to a single magnitude comparison $R \ge B$ (vs. decimal's $0$–$9$ digit guess); trial-subtraction uses [[BinarySubtraction|Ch 4.4.2 subtraction]]; worked example $\mathtt{1011}_2 \div \mathtt{11}_2$ (11 ÷ 3) → quotient $\mathtt{0011}_2 = 3$, remainder $\mathtt{10}_2 = 2$. Restates **integer-division truncation** explicitly — *"in most languages (for example, C, Python 2, and Java) the fractional portion of the result gets truncated"* — supplying the binary-level mechanism behind the [[IntegerDivision|integer-division]] trap [[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]] introduced at the C-language level. The `%` modulus operator returns the integer remainder ($11 \% 3 = 2$), completing the [[CArithmeticOperators|C arithmetic-operator]] surface area for integer division. **Hardware-reuse theme continues**: addition (Ch 4.4.1) / subtraction (Ch 4.4.2) / multiplication (partial-product summation) / division (trial-subtraction) all share the same $N$-bit adder core. **Explicitly NOT covered** by Ch 4.4.3: hardware multipliers (Booth's algorithm / Wallace trees), hardware dividers (restoring / SRT), the [[BitShift|bit-shift]] power-of-two shortcut (multiply by $2^k$ = left-shift $k$; divide by $2^k$ = right-shift $k$), signed-multiplication sign handling, division-by-zero trap behaviour, multiplication overflow rules. **2 new concept pages** ([[BinaryMultiplication]], [[BinaryDivision]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **41 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.4.2 Subtraction](sources/dis-4-4-2-subtraction.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.4.2** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **second subsection** of [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4 *Binary Integer Arithmetic*]]. Delivers the headline **hardware-reuse insight**: subtraction is implemented as **addition of the [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] negation** — *"subtracting $7 - 3$ is equivalent to expressing the operation as $7 + (-3)$"* — so the existing [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]] [[BinaryAddition|adder]] serves subtraction with **no new arithmetic hardware**. The *flip-all-bits-and-add-one* [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] negation recipe ([[dis-4-3-signed|Ch 4.3]]) splits cleanly across the adder's existing inputs: the **bit-flip** is a row of [[XOR|XOR]] gates on operand B; the **add one** is delivered for free by setting [[CarryIn|`CarryIn`]] of the least-significant-bit adder to `1` — cashing in the architectural hook [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]] flagged with *"this feature becomes critical for subtraction implementations."* Worked example 1 ($7 - 3$): flip $\mathtt{0b0011}$ to $\mathtt{0b1100}$, add to $\mathtt{0b0111}$ with `CarryIn = 1` → $\mathtt{0b10100}$ → truncate MSB → $\mathtt{0b0100} = 4$. Worked example 2 ($7 - (-3)$): flip $\mathtt{0b1101}$ to $\mathtt{0b0010}$, add to $\mathtt{0b0111}$ with `CarryIn = 1` → $\mathtt{0b1010} = 10$ — same mechanism handles **all four sign combinations** without special-casing. Caveat: in subtraction mode the MSB carry-out *"doesn't necessarily indicate overflow"* — its meaning differs from the addition case; full [[IntegerOverflow|overflow]] rule deferred. **1 new concept page** ([[BinarySubtraction]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **40 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.4.1 Addition](sources/dis-4-4-1-addition.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.4.1** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **first subsection** of [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4 *Binary Integer Arithmetic*]]. Instantiates the chapter-level interpretation-invariance thesis on the column-by-column [[BinaryAddition|binary addition]] algorithm — *decimal long-addition transfers directly to base 2, only the base changes from $10$ to $2$*. Headline observation: because the only multi-bit elementary sum is $1 + 1 = \mathtt{0b10}$, every column produces at most a **one-bit [[Carry|carry]]** into the next position — strictly simpler than decimal (where carries can be any digit $0$–$9$). Introduces the **eight-row [[FullAdder|full-adder]] truth table** (`DigitA` × `DigitB` × `CarryIn` → `Sum` + `CarryOut`; `Sum = XOR`, `CarryOut = majority`) as the per-bit primitive [[ComputerHardware|hardware]] implements. Worked example $\mathtt{0b0010} + \mathtt{0b1011} = \mathtt{0b1101}$ — position 1's $1+1$ carries into position 2; result reads as **13** ([[UnsignedInteger|unsigned]]) or **−3** ([[TwosComplement|two's complement]]) per [[dis-4-3-signed|Ch 4.3]]'s negative-weight MSB rule, making interpretation-invariance concrete on one bit pattern. Names the [[CarryOut|carry-out]] from the MSB as the bit *"the hardware simply drops or truncates"* — the silent-overflow root mechanism that subsequent Ch 4 sections will formalize as [[IntegerOverflow|integer overflow]]. [[CarryIn|Carry-in]] at the rightmost position is implicit `0` for standard addition but **exists architecturally** because [[BinarySubtraction|subtraction]] sets it to `1` to deliver the *add one* half of [[TwosComplement|two's complement]]'s *flip-and-add-one* negation recipe (preview of [[dis-4-4-2-subtraction|Ch 4.4.2]]). **2 new concept pages** ([[BinaryAddition]], [[Carry]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **39 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.4 Binary Integer Arithmetic](sources/dis-4-4-arithmetic.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.4** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **hub page** for the three-subsection [[BinaryArithmetic|binary integer arithmetic]] block (4.4.1 Addition / 4.4.2 Subtraction / 4.4.3 Multiplication & Division). Headline thesis: decimal place-value arithmetic algorithms transfer directly to [[BinaryNumber|binary]] (only the base changes from $10$ to $2$), and — crucially — *"it does not matter to the arithmetic procedures whether we choose to interpret the operands or result as signed or unsigned"* — the signed/unsigned **interpretation-invariance** that lets [[ComputerHardware|hardware]] designers build a single [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] adder serving both [[UnsignedInteger|unsigned]] and [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] operands. Operational pay-off of [[dis-4-3-signed|Ch 4.3]]'s negative-weight MSB encoding: the bit-level steps are identical across encodings; only the post-hoc interpretation of the result bits differs. Worked algorithms (carry propagation, *"flip and add one"* subtraction, shift-and-add multiplication) delegated to the 4.4.1 / 4.4.2 / 4.4.3 subsection pages. No new concept pages at the hub level. [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **38 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.3 Signed Binary Integers](sources/dis-4-3-signed.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.3** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **signed-encoding extension** of [[dis-4-1-bases|Ch 4.1]]'s unsigned-only treatment. Codifies the two historical [[SignedInteger|signed-integer]] encodings: [[SignMagnitude|sign-magnitude]] (presented as historical context only — *"no modern systems use signed magnitude"* — with the dual-zero pathology `0b0000 = +0`, `0b1000 = −0` as the disqualifier) and [[TwosComplement|two's complement]] (the universal modern standard — the [[MostSignificantBit|MSB]] becomes a place-value digit with **negative weight** $-2^{N-1}$, formula $-(d_{N-1} \cdot 2^{N-1}) + \sum_{i<N-1} d_i \cdot 2^i$, unique zero, asymmetric range $[-2^{N-1},\,2^{N-1}-1]$ with one more negative than positive). Headline negation recipe: *"flip all the bits and add one"* — worked example $13 = $ `0b00001101` → flip to `0b11110010` → add 1 → `0b11110011 = −13`. Adds the [[SignExtension|sign-extension]] rule for widening signed values across bit widths (replicate the high-order bit — non-negatives prepend zeros, negatives prepend ones — preserving both sign and magnitude). **[[OnesComplement|One's complement]] is not covered** — the chapter jumps directly from sign-magnitude to two's complement. **5 new concept pages** ([[SignedInteger]], [[TwosComplement]], [[SignBit]], [[SignMagnitude]], [[SignExtension]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **37 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.2 Converting Between Bases](sources/dis-4-2-conversion.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.2** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **mechanics companion** to [[dis-4-1-bases|Ch 4.1]]. Operationalizes the positional-notation framework $\sum d_i \cdot B^i$ as four concrete [[BaseConversion|base-conversion]] algorithms: (1) **base-$B$ → decimal** via direct evaluation of the place-value sum (`0b110100110 = 422`, `0x9F = 159`); (2) **decimal → base-$B$ via powers-of-target-base** subtraction ($9742 \to$ `0x260E` by walking $4096, 256, 16, 1$); (3) **decimal → base-$B$ via [[RepeatedDivisionMethod|repeated division]]** with bottom-up remainder collection — for $B = 2$ this simplifies to *"if the value is even, the next bit is 0; if odd, the next bit is 1"* ($422 \to$ `0b110100110`); (4) **[[BinaryHexConversion|binary ↔ hex]] per-nibble table lookup** exploiting $16 = 2^4$ — `0xB491 ↔ 1011 0100 1001 0001` with no arithmetic. Octal works the same way with 3-bit groupings ($8 = 2^3$), but hex dominates on modern 8/16/32/64-bit aligned hardware. Frames methods 2 and 3 as **interchangeable** — powers-of-$B$ wins when you've memorized $B^k$, repeated division wins for unfamiliar bases or programmatic implementation. **4 new concept pages** ([[BaseConversion]], [[BinaryHexConversion]], [[RepeatedDivisionMethod]], [[PositionalNotation]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **36 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.10 Exercises](sources/dis-4-10-exercises.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.10** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the exercise set that **fully closes Ch 4 *Binary and Data Representation***. Four problems drilling [[NumberBase|number-base]] conversion: `0b01001010` → decimal/hex; `389` → binary/hex; **base-5** `1423` → decimal (first non-power-of-2 base exercise — exercises [[PositionalNotation]] in the generic $\sum d_i \cdot B^i$ form); plus an interactive *Number Conversion* problem set on the book's external platform. **Structural sibling of [[dis-1-8-exercises|Ch 1.8]] / [[dis-2-11-exercises|Ch 2.11]]** — redirect-to-interactive-platform pattern. Drills [[dis-4-2-conversion|Ch 4.2]]'s four routes ([[BaseConversion|place-value sum]], [[RepeatedDivisionMethod|repeated division]], powers-of-target subtraction, [[BinaryHexConversion|per-nibble lookup]]). No new conceptual material. **47th ingested chapter — fully closes Ch 4.**
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.9 Summary](sources/dis-4-9-summary.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.9** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — short, no-new-material recap closing the prose body of Ch 4 *Binary and Data Representation*. Restates the foundational thesis *"a computer's memory stores all information as binary 0's and 1's"* and recaps the eight-section arc: [[UnsignedInteger|unsigned]] → [[SignedInteger|signed]] integers; arithmetic + [[BitwiseOperator|bitwise]] ops; [[IntegerOverflow|overflow]] as the *"storage space isn't large enough"* hazard; [[FloatingPoint|floating-point]] reals with the *"sacrifice precision for increased flexibility"* trade-off. **Structural sibling of [[dis-1-7-summary|Ch 1.7]] / [[dis-2-10-summary|Ch 2.10]] / [[dis-3-7-summary|Ch 3.7]]**. No new concept pages. 46th ingested chapter.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.8 Real Numbers in Binary](sources/dis-4-8-floating-point.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.8** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — extends Ch 4's binary-representation arc from integers to **real numbers**, opening with the impossibility result *"for any binary encoding of real numbers, there exist values that cannot be represented exactly."* Surveys two encodings: **[[FixedPoint|fixed-point]]** (extends [[UnsignedInteger|unsigned-integer]] place-value to negative powers of 2 at a pinned binary point — `0b000101.10 = 5.5`) and **[[FloatingPoint|floating-point]]** under the **[[IEEE754|IEEE 754]] 32-bit standard** (1-bit [[SignBit|sign]] / 8-bit biased [[Exponent|exponent]] / 23-bit [[Mantissa|significand]] with implicit leading 1 — *"the significand gets multiplied by $2^{\text{exponent} - 127}$, where the 127 is a bias"* — worked example `0b11000001101101000000000000000000 = -22.5`). Headline shared pathology: **rounding makes arithmetic non-associative** — under truncation $(0.75 / 2) \cdot 3 = 0.75$ but $(0.75 \cdot 3) / 2 = 1.00$ where the exact answer is $1.125$. Two cited real-world catastrophes: the **1991 Patriot missile** failure in Dhahran (accumulated $0.1 \cdot$ time-counter rounding drift → Scud-interception miss → 28 dead U.S. soldiers) and the **1996 Ariane 5** explosion 39 seconds after launch (64-bit-float → 16-bit-signed-int [[IntegerOverflow|conversion overflow]] — the [[dis-4-5-overflow|Ch 4.5]] phenomenon striking at the float-to-int boundary). **Explicit scope omissions** (wiki-flagged): no 64-bit `binary64`, no denormals / [[NaN|NaN]] / $\pm\infty$, no rounding-mode enumeration, no machine-epsilon. **5 new concept pages** ([[FloatingPoint]], [[IEEE754]], [[Mantissa]], [[Exponent]], [[FixedPoint]], [[FloatingPointPrecision]] — 6 total). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **45 chapters** — **Ch 4 *Binary and Data Representation* fully complete** (4.1 bases / 4.2 conversion / 4.3 signed / 4.4 arithmetic / 4.5 overflow / 4.6 bitwise / 4.7 byte order / **4.8 real numbers**).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.7 Integer Byte Order](sources/dis-4-7-byte-order.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.7** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **memory-layout section** that closes Ch 4 *Binary and Data Representation* by codifying **[[ByteOrder|byte order]]** ([[Endianness|endianness]]): how the [[Byte|bytes]] of a multibyte integer are laid out across consecutive [[MemoryAddress|memory addresses]]. *"Byte order, sometimes referred to as endianness, describes the order in which the bytes of a multibyte value are ordered in memory."* Distinguishes **[[BigEndian|big-endian]]** (MSByte at lowest address — matches left-to-right written numerals; used by [[PowerPC]] / [[SPARC]] / [[Motorola68k]] / mainframes / network protocols) from **[[LittleEndian|little-endian]]** (LSByte at lowest address — appears reversed; used by [[X86]] / [[X86_64]] / [[ARM]] / [[RISCV|RISC-V]] — virtually all deployed modern CPUs as of 2025). Demonstrates with a [[CCast|`char *` cast]] over `int value = 0xAABBCCDD;` — on x86 the bytes walk out as `DD CC BB AA`, **proof of little-endian storage**. Three canonical scenarios where endianness leaks out of the [[Abstraction|abstraction]]: (1) **network transmission** — *"The IETF defines big-endian as the network byte order"*, the standardization that makes [[TCPIP|TCP/IP]] interoperable regardless of host endianness ([[POSIX]] supplies [[Htonl|`htonl` / `ntohl` / `htons` / `ntohs`]] in `<arpa/inet.h>`); (2) **file formats** — binary files written on one host and read on another with different endianness yield garbage unless the format pins endianness ([[JPEG]] big-endian, [[BMP]] / [[WAV]] little-endian, [[TIFF]] declares per-file); (3) **debugger / raw-memory inspection** — `gdb`'s [[GdbExamineMemory|`x/4xb`]] shows reversed bytes on little-endian hosts. Architecture map: [[X86]] always little-endian; [[ARM]] / [[MIPS]] / [[PowerPC]] are technically [[BiEndian|bi-endian]] but virtually always run little-endian in deployment ([[POWER8]]+ on Linux flipped to little-endian to ease x86 porting). Etymology: Jonathan Swift's *[[GulliversTravels|Gulliver's Travels]]* (1726) via [[DannyCohen|Danny Cohen]]'s 1980 [[IETF]] IEN-137 memo *On Holy Wars and a Plea for Peace*. **Closes Ch 4 *Binary and Data Representation***: Ch 4.1–4.6 treated multibyte integers as undifferentiated bit-strings; Ch 4.7 adds the address-level layout dimension that matters at cross-machine / cross-file / cross-wire boundaries. **4 new concept pages** ([[ByteOrder]] umbrella, [[Endianness]] alias, [[BigEndian]], [[LittleEndian]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **44 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.6 Bitwise Operators](sources/dis-4-6-bitwise.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.6** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **operator-surface section** that exposes [[CLanguage|C]]'s six [[BitwiseOperator|bitwise operators]] (`&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`) as the per-bit primitives that *"directly apply [[LogicGate|logic-gate]] behavior to bit sequences"*. Bridges from Ch 4.1–4.5's value-level [[BinaryRepresentation|binary representation]] and [[BinaryArithmetic|integer arithmetic]] into the **bit-manipulation idioms** systems code uses: **[[BitwiseAnd|AND `&`]]** (masking — `26 & 54 = 18`); **[[BitwiseOr|OR `|`]]** (setting bits — `26 | 54 = 62`); **[[BitwiseXor|XOR `^`]]** (toggling / difference detection — `26 ^ 54 = 44`); **[[BitwiseNot|NOT `~`]]** (inverting — `~26 = -27` because *"bitwise NOT only flips the bits and doesn't add one"* — one short of [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] negation, hence the `~x = -x - 1` identity); **left shift `<<`** (zero-fill from right, truncate at MSB — multiplication by $2^N$, `13 << 3 = 104`); **right shift `>>`** — **the [[LogicalRightShift|logical]] / [[ArithmeticRightShift|arithmetic]] split** dispatched by operand type: [[UnsignedInteger|unsigned]] → zero-fill ([[LogicalRightShift|logical]] — `0xFF000000 >> 12 = 0x000FF000`); signed → replicate [[SignBit|sign bit]] ([[ArithmeticRightShift|arithmetic] — `0xFF000000 >> 12 = 0xFFFFF000`), *"The C compiler automatically selects the appropriate shifting variant based on variable declaration."* Names the **canonical category error**: *"programmers often confuse the bitwise `&&` and `||` operators with `&` and `|` operators"* — the [[LogicalOperator|logical operators]] short-circuit on truth values; the bitwise operators act per bit on the operand width. Codifies the **bit-test / set / clear / toggle / mask** idioms (`x & (1<<i)` / `x |= (1<<i)` / `x &= ~(1<<i)` / `x ^= (1<<i)` / `(x >> shift) & ((1<<width) - 1)`). Hardware payoff: bitwise operators map **one-to-one onto [[LogicGate|logic gates]]** (AND / OR / XOR / NOT) and execute in **one clock cycle with no carry propagation** — the cheapest ops in the [[InstructionSetArchitecture|ISA]]; shifts implement as a **barrel-shifter** switch network. **Closes the [[dis-4-4-3-mult-div|Ch 4.4.3]]-deferred *"bit-shift power-of-two shortcut"*** for multiplication and division (`x * 16 = x << 4`; `x / 16 = x >> 4` unsigned), the **strength-reduction** pattern compilers apply automatically. **Scope notes**: rotation operators (`ROL` / `ROR`), [[CStruct|struct]] bit-fields, popcount / clz / ctz / bswap intrinsics, the XOR-swap idiom, and shift UB rules (shift-by-≥-width, signed-shift-overflow) are out of chapter scope; wiki page records the C-level UB pitfalls. **2 new concept pages** ([[BitwiseOperator]], [[BitShift]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **43 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.1 Number Bases and Unsigned Integers](sources/dis-4-1-bases.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.1** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **opens Ch 4 *Binary and Data Representation***, the book's first descent below [[CLanguage|C]] into how data is encoded in [[ComputerHardware|hardware]]. Codifies positional [[NumberBase|number bases]] via the place-value sum $\sum d_i \cdot B^i$ and instantiates it for **decimal (base 10)**, **[[BinaryNumber|binary (base 2)]]** (`0b1000 = 8`, `0b10110100 = 180`), **[[OctalNumber|octal (base 8)]]**, and **[[HexadecimalNumber|hexadecimal (base 16)]]** (`0x23C8 = 9160`). Introduces the [[CLanguage|C]]-source [[BasePrefix|base prefixes]] **`0b`** (binary) / **`0`** or **`0o`** (octal) / **`0x`** (hexadecimal) and the [[UnsignedInteger|unsigned-integer]] $[0,\,2^N-1]$ range rule (8-bit `unsigned char` holds `0`–`255`). Because $16 = 2^4$ and $8 = 2^3$, one hex digit packs 4 bits and one octal digit packs 3 bits — the reason hex dominates as the compact display form for [[BinaryRepresentation|binary data]]. Signed encodings explicitly deferred to subsequent Ch 4 sections. **Opens Ch 4** after the seven-section Ch 3 *C Debugging Tools* block closed with [[dis-3-7-summary|Ch 3.7]]. **6 new concept pages** ([[NumberBase]], [[BinaryNumber]], [[HexadecimalNumber]], [[OctalNumber]], [[UnsignedInteger]], [[BasePrefix]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **35 chapters**.

Short, no-new-material recap that restates [[dis-0-introduction|Ch 0]]'s thesis — *"C is a relatively small programming language with a few basic constructs"* whose abstractions sit *"closer to the underlying machine code"*, yielding efficiency and programmer-controlled memory layout, *"the language of computer systems programming."* Structural sibling of [[dis-1-7-summary|Ch 1.7 Summary]] and [[dis-2-10-summary|Ch 2.10 Summary]] — same recap-at-chapter-end role. Implicitly retires [[dis-2-10-summary|Ch 2.10]]'s two-debugging-tools promise — both [[GDB]] (Ch 3.1 + 3.2 + 3.4 + 3.5 + 3.6) and [[Valgrind]] (Ch 3.3) now delivered. - [Dive into Systems — Ch 3.6 Debugging Multi-threaded Programs](sources/dis-3-6-gdb-pthreads.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 3.6** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **closes Ch 3 *C Debugging Tools*** by extending the [[GDB]] block from single-threaded to multi-threaded programs. Frames concurrent debugging as fundamentally harder (multiple execution streams, thread interactions, non-determinism) with three practical mitigations: minimize active thread count during development, include the thread ID in debug output, scope verbose logging to one thread. Introduces the **[[GDB]] thread-debugging vocabulary** layered on [[Pthreads]]: (1) [[GdbInfoThreads|`info threads`]] — enumerate all active threads (`*` marks current); (2) [[GdbThreadSwitch|`thread <N>`]] — switch the inspection context to a specific thread's [[StackFrame|stack]] / [[LocalVariable|locals]] / [[CpuRegister|registers]] (multi-thread analog of [[GdbBacktrace|`frame N`]]); (3) **thread-qualified breakpoints** via `break <loc> thread <N>` — fire only for the named thread; (4) [[GdbThreadApply|`thread apply all <cmd>`]] — broadcast a [[GDB]] command across every thread, canonical use `thread apply all bt` for the **deadlock-diagnostic** multi-thread call-stack snapshot; (5) [[GdbSet|`set print thread-events`]] / [[GdbSet|`set scheduler-locking`]] for thread-lifecycle notifications and stop-the-world override. Names [[GDB]]'s **three thread identifiers** ([[Pthreads|`pthread_t`]] / kernel **LWP ID** / **GDB thread number**), each with typical 1:1 correspondence. Notes the default **stop-the-world breakpoint** behaviour (*"by default, reaching any breakpoint pauses all threads"*) and the scheduler-locking flip for observing real concurrency. Worked example: five threads racing on shared `count += i` with thread-qualified breakpoints surfaces the [[RaceCondition|race-condition]] symptom. **Promotes [[Pthreads]] from cross-corpus stub to first-class DIS concept** (DIS's first Pthreads sighting; full coverage deferred to Ch 14). **4 new concept pages** ([[GdbInfoThreads]], [[GdbThreadSwitch]], [[GdbThreadApply]]) + [[Pthreads]] entity in-place update. - [Dive into Systems — Ch 3.5 Debugging Assembly Code](sources/dis-3-5-gdb-assembly.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 3.5** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — drops the [[GDB]] block to the **[[AssemblyLanguage|assembly-instruction]] level**. Names the [[InstructionPointer|`%rip` / `%eip`]] register as the assembly-level *"you are here"* marker — alias `$pc` works across [[ISA|ISAs]]. Closes by recommending [[DataDisplayDebugger|DDD]]'s separate disassembly / register / command panes for the multi-pane workflow. The escape hatch when [[CompilerOptimization|`-O2`]] / stripped binaries / hand-written `.s` ([[dis-2-9-7-c-to-assembly|Ch 2.9.7]]) make the source view inadequate. **4 new concept pages** ([[GdbDisassemble]], [[GdbStepi]], [[CpuRegister]], [[InstructionPointer]]). - [Dive into Systems — Ch 3.4 Advanced GDB Features](sources/dis-3-4-gdb-advanced.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 3.4** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **advanced-workflows extension** to the [[dis-3-1-gdb|Ch 3.1]] / [[dis-3-2-gdb-commands|Ch 3.2]] [[GDB]] block. Surfaces the workflows **beyond *"compile, run, set breakpoints, step, print"*** — the cross-process, signal-driven, and `fork()`-aware features that turn [[GDB]] from a single-program debugger into a tool for **already-running**, **signal-handling**, and **multi-process** programs. Five short sections, each a self-contained workflow: (1) **[[GDB]] ↔ `make` integration** — running `make` from inside the [[GDB]] session preserves the [[Breakpoint|breakpoint]] list across rebuilds (*"GDB accepts the `make` command to rebuild an executable during a debugging session"*); (2) **[[GdbAttach|attaching to a running process]]** via `gdb <executable> <pid>` (PID discovered with [[Ps|`ps -A | grep`]]) — the [[Ptrace]]-backed user-side primitive for debugging long-running services / daemons / heisenbugs, with the **self-pause idiom** `kill(getpid(), SIGSTOP)` as the corpus's first **debugger-aware program design** pattern; (3) **[[GdbFollowFork|`set follow-fork-mode child` / `parent`]]** — *"by default, GDB follows the parent after a call to `fork()`"* — chooses which side of a [[Fork|`fork()`]]ed program [[GDB]] follows, the headline primitive for **multi-process debugging** the corpus has been building toward; (4) **[[GdbSignalControl|signal control]]** — `signal SIGCONT` / `signal SIGUSR1` to **send** [[Signal|signals]] to the debuggee, `handle SIGBUS stop` to **intercept** [[Signal|signals]] in [[GDB]], `info signal` / `info SIGALRM` to inspect handling rules — names [[SIGBUS]] as the canonical alignment-fault scenario distinct from [[SegmentationFault|`SIGSEGV`]] (*"if a program tries to access memory with a misaligned memory address for the type it is accessing, it receives a `SIGBUS` signal"*); (5) **[[DataDisplayDebugger|DDD]] settings reset** — `rm -rf ~/.ddd` to fix the *"Waiting until GDB ready"* startup hang. **6 new concept pages** ([[GdbAttach]], [[GdbFollowFork]], [[GdbSignalControl]], [[Ps]], [[Fork]], [[Signal]], [[SIGBUS]], [[Kill]] — 8 total) + [[DataDisplayDebugger]] in-place update note. Closes the *Dive into Systems* [[GDB]] coverage with the **systems-level features** ([[Ptrace|`ptrace`]] / [[Fork|`fork()`]] / [[Signal|signals]]) that distinguish [[GDB]] from a simple line-stepper — formal coverage of those kernel primitives deferred to Ch 9+. - [Dive into Systems — Ch 3.3 Debugging Memory with Valgrind](sources/dis-3-3-valgrind.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 3.3** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 3 *C Debugging Tools* — **the second of the two debugging tools** [[dis-2-10-summary|Ch 2.10]] forward-referenced (the first being [[GDB]] in [[dis-3-1-gdb|Ch 3.1]] / [[dis-3-2-gdb-commands|Ch 3.2]]). Introduces [[Valgrind]] and its default tool [[Memcheck]] as the **heap-memory-error detector** complementing [[GDB]]'s general-purpose [[Debugger|debugger]] role — *"Valgrind's Memcheck debugging tool highlights heap memory errors in programs."* Catalogues the **four heap-error classes** [[Memcheck]] catches: [[UninitializedReadError|uninitialized reads]] (e.g., `x = ptr[3]` before assignment), **invalid memory access** (*"reading or writing a value at an unallocated memory location, which often indicates an array out-of-bounds error"* — heap-side [[BufferOverflow|buffer overflow]]), [[UseAfterFree|use-after-free]] including *"freeing already freed memory"* ([[DoubleFree|double-free]]), and [[MemoryLeak|memory leaks]] (*"a chunk of allocated heap memory space that is not referred to by any pointer variable in the program, and thus it cannot be freed"*). Operationalizes the workflow: [[GccDashG|`gcc -g`]] then `valgrind -v ./a.out` (default tool = memcheck; redirect with `>& output.txt`; add `--leak-check=yes` for per-leak stack traces). Codifies the **three-part error-message anatomy** (error type/size + access stack trace + allocation-site stack trace, all `==PID==`-tagged) and the **explicit scope boundary**: *"Valgrind does not detect stack memory access errors at the same granularity as it does with heap memory, and it does not detect memory access errors with global data memory."* Recommends pairing with [[GDB]] — set a [[Breakpoint|breakpoint]] at Valgrind's flagged line, [[GdbBacktrace|`bt`]] / [[GdbPrint|`print`]] for root cause. **Promotes [[Valgrind]] from forward-ref stub to first-class tool**; introduces 3 new concept pages ([[Valgrind]], [[Memcheck]], [[UninitializedReadError]]) + 1 wiki-only treatment ([[AddressSanitizer]] — not in the chapter but the canonical modern alternative).
