- [Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT)](concepts/SimultaneousMultithreading.md) — [[HardwareMultithreading|Hardware-multithreading]] variant that **issues instructions from multiple threads in the same clock cycle** — uses the wide-issue capability of [[Superscalar|superscalar]] hardware to fill issue slots a single thread alone could not. **Requires superscalar issue** (you cannot co-issue without multi-issue hardware) — distinguishes SMT from interleaved multithreading, which time-slices threads on the same pipeline. **Per-chip IPC examples** (Ch 5.9 tables): **IBM Power 9** (24 cores × **8-way SMT** → IPC **192**); **Oracle SPARC M7** (32 × 8 → IPC 64). Per Ch 5.9, **Intel's [[HyperThreading|Hyper-Threading]] implements interleaved multithreading, not true SMT**. ([[dis-5-9-modern]]).
- [Hyper-Threading](concepts/HyperThreading.md) — Intel's commercial [[HardwareMultithreading|hardware-multithreading]] technology, exposing **two logical threads per physical core** to the [[OperatingSystem|operating system]]. **Ch 5.9's pedagogical clarification**: Hyper-Threading implements **interleaved** multithreading (one thread issues per cycle, alternating), **not** [[SimultaneousMultithreading|true SMT]] (which would co-issue from both threads in the same cycle). Hyper-Threading still hides latency by filling pipeline slots wasted by stalls — but it does **not** push per-core IPC above 1 the way true [[SimultaneousMultithreading|SMT]] (e.g. IBM Power 9's 8-way SMT) does. ([[dis-5-9-modern]]).
- [GPGPU (General-Purpose GPU Computing)](concepts/GPGPU.md) — The use of GPUs as massively-parallel compute accelerators for workloads beyond rendering. Ch 5.9's specific framing: GPU accelerators are **the modern home of the [[VectorProcessor|vector-processor]] [[InstructionLevelParallelism|ILP]] model** — the architectural lineage that started with the [[Cray1|Cray-1]] (1976) and ceded the general-purpose CPU market to [[Superscalar|superscalar]] designs has not disappeared, it has **migrated**: *"vector processors today primarily appear in GPU accelerators."* A modern GPU streaming multiprocessor is, structurally, a wide vector machine: many lanes executing the same instruction on different data — generalized for graphics-shader workloads and now reused for everything from physics simulation to neural-network inference. ([[dis-5-9-modern]]).

### Added with [[dis-5-8-pipelining-advanced]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 5.8 Advanced Pipelining Considerations)

- [Pipeline Hazard](concepts/PipelineHazard.md) — Umbrella concept for situations where two in-flight instructions interfere with each other in a pipelined [[CPU]] — breaking [[dis-5-7-pipelining|Ch 5.7]]'s *"one instruction per cycle"* assumption. Ch 5.8 covers two categories: [[DataHazard|data hazards]] (register-dependency interference) and [[ControlHazard|control hazards]] (branch-resolution interference). Mitigated by [[PipelineStall|stalling]] / [[Forwarding|forwarding]] / [[BranchPrediction|branch prediction]] / eager execution. ([[dis-5-8-pipelining-advanced]]).
- [Data Hazard](concepts/DataHazard.md) — [[PipelineHazard|Hazard]] where *"two instructions attempt to access common data in an instruction pipeline"* — e.g. a `MOV` writing a register and the immediately-following `ADD` reading it before the `MOV`'s WriteBack completes. Mitigated by [[PipelineStall|bubbles]] (simple, costly) or [[Forwarding|operand forwarding]] (the bypass-the-register-file wire that *"reads the result from the previous operation"*). ([[dis-5-8-pipelining-advanced]]).
- [Control Hazard](concepts/ControlHazard.md) — [[PipelineHazard|Hazard]] from a [[BranchInstruction|branch (conditional) instruction]] in the pipeline — the processor cannot determine which instruction comes next until the branch resolves; speculatively-fetched instructions may need flushing. Mitigated by stall-until-resolved, [[BranchPrediction|branch prediction]] (the dominant choice — but introduces speculative-execution vulnerabilities like [[Spectre]]), or eager execution of both paths. ([[dis-5-8-pipelining-advanced]]).
- [Branch Prediction](concepts/BranchPrediction.md) — *"The most common solution"* to [[ControlHazard|control hazards]] — guess the branch direction from history and speculatively fetch from the predicted target; flush on misprediction. Achieves high accuracy on modern CPUs but introduced the speculative-execution side-channel attack class exemplified by **[[Spectre]]**. ([[dis-5-8-pipelining-advanced]]).
- [Branch Predictor](concepts/BranchPredictor.md) — The named hardware structure that implements [[BranchPrediction|branch prediction]]: inputs branch-execution history, outputs a taken/not-taken prediction driving speculative [[PipelineStages|Fetch]]. Ch 5.8 introduces the role of the predictor; specific algorithms (bimodal / two-bit / gshare / TAGE / perceptron) out of scope. ([[dis-5-8-pipelining-advanced]]).
- [Operand Forwarding (Bypassing)](concepts/Forwarding.md) — Hardware mitigation for [[DataHazard|data hazards]] that **avoids the stall** by wiring the producing instruction's stage output directly into the consuming instruction's stage input — so the consumer sees the correct value before the producer's WriteBack completes. *"Rather than stalling, the pipeline reads the result from the previous operation."* The preferred mitigation when applicable; keeps effective [[CyclesPerInstruction|CPI]] near 1. ([[dis-5-8-pipelining-advanced]]).
- [Pipeline Stall (Bubble)](concepts/PipelineStall.md) — Simplest [[PipelineHazard|hazard]] mitigation: the processor *"forces all instructions to take the same number of pipeline stages by inserting [[NoOperation|no-operation]] instructions for stages not needed."* Each stall cycle is a wasted slot — pushes effective [[CyclesPerInstruction|CPI]] back above 1. Used against [[DataHazard|data hazards]] when [[Forwarding|forwarding]] is unavailable and against [[ControlHazard|control hazards]] when [[BranchPrediction|prediction]] is unavailable or has just mispredicted. ([[dis-5-8-pipelining-advanced]]).
- [Superscalar Execution](concepts/Superscalar.md) — Performance layer on top of [[InstructionPipelining|pipelining]] that **replicates** stage circuitry so multiple instructions can occupy the *same* stage in the *same* cycle — pushing [[InstructionThroughput|IPC]] above 1 (equivalently [[CyclesPerInstruction|CPI]] below 1). Orthogonal to pipelining: pipelining parallelizes across time, superscalar across space — real CPUs combine both. ([[dis-5-8-pipelining-advanced]]).
- [Out-of-Order Execution](concepts/OutOfOrderExecution.md) — Performance layer on top of [[InstructionPipelining|pipelining]] that dynamically **reorders** in-flight instructions — when one is stalled (slow operand, cache miss, long-latency op), the CPU runs **later** ready-to-execute instructions, then commits results in program order at retirement. Combined with [[Superscalar|superscalar]] issue, gives modern CPUs their dispatch-many-find-ready scheduling story. ([[dis-5-8-pipelining-advanced]]).

### Added with [[dis-5-7-pipelining]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 5.7 Pipelining Instruction Execution)

- [Instruction Pipelining](concepts/InstructionPipelining.md) — CPU-microarchitecture technique that **overlaps execution of successive instructions** across the four [[FetchDecodeExecuteCycle|fetch-decode-execute]] stages — starting a new instruction every [[ClockCycle|cycle]] rather than waiting for the current one to finish. Cashes in the **stage-specific idleness** of the non-pipelined baseline (each stage sits unused 3 of every 4 cycles). Headline result: once full, the pipeline yields **one instruction completion per cycle** — effective [[CyclesPerInstruction|CPI]] → 1 — **without reducing per-instruction latency**. Trade-off: additional per-stage storage + control circuitry. ARM 3+ stages; Intel Core i7 14 stages. ([[dis-5-7-pipelining]]).
- [Pipeline Stages](concepts/PipelineStages.md) — Discrete steps a pipelined [[CPU]] decomposes instruction execution into — each backed by **disjoint stage-specific circuitry** that can work on a different in-flight instruction every [[ClockCycle|cycle]]. Two canonical Ch 5.7 decompositions: the **four-stage** Fetch → Decode → Execute → WriteBack (for register-only instructions) and the **five-stage** Fetch → Decode → Execute → Memory → WriteBack (for loads and stores that touch [[RAM|memory]]). Stage circuitry doesn't overlap (Fetch uses PC + memory-read; Decode uses [[InstructionRegister|IR]]-parsing + register-file read ports; Execute uses the [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]]; WriteBack uses the register-file write port) — the structural property [[InstructionPipelining|pipelining]] exploits. ([[dis-5-7-pipelining]]).
- [Instruction Throughput](concepts/InstructionThroughput.md) — Rate at which a [[CPU]] **completes** instructions — measured in instructions per [[ClockCycle|clock cycle]] in [[dis-5-7-pipelining|Ch 5.7]]. The **performance metric [[InstructionPipelining|pipelining]] optimizes**, sharply distinguished from per-instruction **latency**: pipelining leaves end-to-end latency at four cycles per instruction but drives steady-state throughput from ~1/4 (non-pipelined) to ~1 (full pipeline). Related to [[CyclesPerInstruction|CPI]] as inverse rate; overall performance ≈ [[ClockSpeed|clock rate]] × throughput. ([[dis-5-7-pipelining]]).

### Added with [[dis-5-6-instruction-execution]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 5.6 The Processor's Execution of Program Instructions)

- [Instruction Set](concepts/InstructionSet.md) — The catalog of operations a [[CPU]] can execute (a.k.a. **ISA** — instruction set architecture). The **hardware/software contract**: each instruction has an [[OpCode|opcode]] (operation-naming bit field) plus operand fields (register selectors, immediates, addressing-mode bits) laid out in an ISA-defined format that the [[ControlCircuit|control circuits]] are wired to decode. An $N$-operation ISA needs $\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ opcode bits (the same MUX-selector arithmetic from [[dis-5-4-2-control-circuits|Ch 5.4.2]]). Also fixes instruction width — a 32-bit ISA increments the [[ProgramCounter|PC]] by 4 per Fetch. ([[dis-5-6-instruction-execution]]).
- [Machine Code](concepts/MachineCode.md) — The binary bit-pattern encoding of an [[InstructionSet|ISA]]'s instructions — **the only language the [[CPU]] directly executes**. Fixed-width in RISC-style ISAs, variable-width in CISC. Each instruction has an [[OpCode|opcode]] field plus operand fields per the ISA's instruction format. Lives in the [[InstructionRegister|IR]] during execution — fetched from the address the [[ProgramCounter|PC]] holds, decoded into opcode + operand fields, executed by the [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]]. Output of the [[AssemblerToMachineCode|assembler]] (or compiler back end); inverse is **disassembly**. ([[dis-5-6-instruction-execution]]).
- [Opcode](concepts/OpCode.md) — Promoted from sibling-page mention in [[dis-5-5-cpu|Ch 5.5]] to **first-class concept page**. The field of a [[MachineCode|machine-code]] instruction that **names the operation** (ADD / SUB / OR / AND / load / store / branch); occupies the high-order bits in typical [[InstructionSet|ISA]] encodings. In Ch 5.5's data path it is one of three [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] inputs (alongside operands A and B) driving the ALU's internal sub-operation-selecting [[Multiplexer|MUX]]; in Ch 5.6 it is **extracted from the [[InstructionRegister|IR]] during Decode** and routed to the ALU. ([[dis-5-5-cpu]] / [[dis-5-6-instruction-execution]]).
- [Assembler-to-Machine-Code Translation](concepts/AssemblerToMachineCode.md) — The toolchain step that converts human-readable [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] mnemonics (e.g. `add r1, r2, r3`) into the [[MachineCode|machine-code]] bit pattern the [[CPU]] actually executes; the program that does it is the **assembler**, and the rules it follows are the target [[InstructionSet|ISA]]'s instruction-format specification. Typically one-to-one mnemonic-to-instruction; pseudo-ops and macros may expand to several. Inverse direction is **disassembly** ([[GDB]] `disassemble`, `objdump`). ([[dis-5-6-instruction-execution]]).

### Added with [[dis-5-5-cpu]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 5.5 Building a Processor)

- [Processor Data Path](concepts/ProcessorDatapath.md) — Ch 5.5's **integration concept**: *"the data path consists of the parts of the CPU that perform arithmetic and logic operations (the ALU) and store data (registers), and the buses that connect these parts"* ([[dis-5-5-cpu|Ch 5.5]] §5.5.3). Wires [[dis-5-4-1-arithmetic-logic-circuits|Ch 5.4.1]]'s [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] + [[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits|Ch 5.4.3]]'s [[RegisterFile|register file]] + [[Bus|buses]] into a single CPU compute-and-store layer. Sibling **control path** named but mechanism deferred to the next section. ([[dis-5-5-cpu]]).
- [Clock Cycle](concepts/ClockCycle.md) — One period of the [[ClockSignal|clock signal]] pacing a synchronous [[CPU]]. Ch 5.5 names the clock role only — *"a clock that drives the circuitry of the CPU to execute program instructions"* — and **defers the quantitative cycle treatment** (period-vs-frequency, what fits inside a cycle, CPI, pipelining) to the next section. **Named-role-only forward-reference page** following the *"only what's covered"* rule. ([[dis-5-5-cpu]]).
- [Clock Speed](concepts/ClockSpeed.md) — Clock **frequency** $f = 1/T$ — reciprocal of the [[ClockCycle|clock-cycle]] period; measured in **Hz** / **GHz** (`1 GHz = 10^9` cycles/s). Ch 5.5 **does not quantify** clock speed, does not introduce Hz / GHz units, and does not discuss its relation to instruction-throughput performance — all forward-referenced. **Named-role-only forward-reference page**. ([[dis-5-5-cpu]]).
- [Circuit Delay](concepts/CircuitDelay.md) — Propagation delay through a combinational [[Circuit|circuit]] — the physical floor on [[ClockCycle|clock-cycle]] length (*clock period ≥ longest combinational-path delay*). Ch 5.5 **does not quantitatively treat** circuit delay; the relevant bound is forward-referenced. Connects to [[dis-5-4-1-arithmetic-logic-circuits|Ch 5.4.1]]'s qualitative observation that the SUM result *"ripples or propagates through the circuit from the low-order to the high-order bits"* in a [[RippleCarryAdder|ripple-carry adder]]. **Named-role-only forward-reference page**. ([[dis-5-5-cpu]]).

### Added with [[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 5.4.3 Storage Circuits)

- [Storage Circuit](concepts/StorageCircuit.md) — Category-level page for the **third** of the three [[Circuit|circuit]] categories ([[dis-5-4-circuits|Ch 5.4]]'s partition). *"A storage circuit's value depends on its input values and also its currently stored value"* ([[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits|Ch 5.4.3]]) — feedback loop is the structural signature distinguishing **sequential** storage from the **combinational** [[ArithmeticLogicCircuit|arithmetic-logic]] and [[ControlCircuit|control]] siblings (where compute / route → here **remember**). Two-technology split: [[SRAM]] (circuit-based, fast, used for [[CpuRegister|registers]] / cache) vs [[DRAM]] (capacitor-based, denser but needs refresh, used for main [[RAM|memory]]). Build-up ladder: [[SRLatch|RS latch]] → [[DLatch|gated D latch]] → [[CpuRegister|N-bit register]] → [[RegisterFile|register file]]. **Promoted from forward-reference to category page — closes Ch 5.4's three-category partition.** ([[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits]]).
- [Latch](concepts/Latch.md) — Generic 1-bit [[StorageCircuit|storage cell]] — **level-sensitive** sequential-logic primitive with a feedback loop. While the control input is asserted the latch is *transparent* and follows its data input; when deasserted it **holds**. Two variants built in [[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits|Ch 5.4.3]]: [[SRLatch|RS latch]] (raw) and [[DLatch|gated D latch]] (safe, [[WriteEnable|WE]]-controlled). The level-sensitive cousin of the [[FlipFlop|edge-triggered flip-flop]] (which the chapter does not build at the gate level — informally calls the D latch a "flip-flop"). ([[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits]]).
- [Flip-Flop](concepts/FlipFlop.md) — In wider digital-design vocabulary an **edge-triggered** 1-bit [[StorageCircuit|storage cell]] (samples on a clock edge, holds otherwise) — distinguishing it from a level-sensitive [[Latch|latch]]. [[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits|Ch 5.4.3]] uses *"flip-flop"* **informally as a [[DLatch|D-latch]] synonym** and **does not build an edge-triggered master-slave construction** — the chapter omits the clock-edge, setup/hold, and master-slave machinery entirely; that treatment is deferred. **Page documents the term as it surfaces in Ch 5.4.3** plus the omitted forward-context. ([[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits]]).
- [RS (Reset-Set) Latch](concepts/SRLatch.md) — The minimal 1-bit [[StorageCircuit|storage cell]]. **Two cross-coupled [[NandGate|NAND]] gates with a feedback loop**; inputs `S` (set) and `R` (reset), output `Q`. Operating modes: `S=R=1` → **hold** (memory mode — *"when S and R are both 1, the latch maintains its current value"* — [[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits|Ch 5.4.3]]); `S=1,R=0` → **reset** to 0; `S=0,R=1` → **set** to 1; `S=R=0` → **forbidden / undefined**. Active-low inputs are the natural consequence of the NAND construction. The forbidden case is precisely why the [[DLatch|gated D latch]] exists — its [[WriteEnable|WE]]-gated front-end makes that input combination structurally unreachable. ([[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits]]).
- [Gated D Latch](concepts/DLatch.md) — The **safe usable 1-bit storage cell**. Wraps an [[SRLatch|RS latch]] in two extra [[NandGate|NAND]] gates forming a control front-end with two inputs: **`D`** (data) and **`WE`** ([[WriteEnable|Write Enable]]). `WE=0` → both internal `R` and `S` forced to `1` → **hold**; `WE=1` → latch loads `D`. *"The gated D latch improves upon the RS latch by adding control circuitry that prevents simultaneous 0 inputs to both R and S"* ([[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits|Ch 5.4.3]]) — the forbidden RS case is **eliminated by construction**. Composes trivially into [[CpuRegister|N-bit registers]] — stack `N` D-latches sharing one `WE`. ([[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits]]).
- [Write Enable (WE)](concepts/WriteEnable.md) — **Single-bit control input** on a writable [[StorageCircuit|storage cell]] gating update-vs-hold. On the [[DLatch|gated D latch]]: `WE=0` forces the underlying [[SRLatch|RS latch]] into hold mode (cell ignores `D`, remembers prior value); `WE=1` drives internal `R`/`S` from `D` and loads it. Discipline scales: an N-bit [[CpuRegister|register]] fans one `WE` wire to all N latches; a K-register [[RegisterFile|register file]] uses a [[Decoder|decoder]] on address bits to assert exactly one register's `WE`. **Stands in for clock-gated write control** — Ch 5.4.3 abstracts the [[ClockSignal|clock]] away, using `WE` as the abstracted control wire a real synchronous CPU would derive as `clock_edge AND register_write_command`. ([[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits]]).
- [Clock Signal](concepts/ClockSignal.md) — Periodic timing wire pacing a synchronous digital circuit, scheduling when [[StorageCircuit|storage elements]] sample inputs. [[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits|Ch 5.4.3]] **abstracts the clock away** — exposes only the single binary [[WriteEnable|`WE`]] control input, sidestepping edge-triggering, master-slave [[FlipFlop|flip-flop]] construction, setup/hold timing, and metastability. **Documents what the chapter elides** (forward-context for later DIS chapters): clock distributes a common timing reference, `WE` is typically derived as `clock_edge AND control`, period is set by the longest critical path, edge-triggered flip-flops give each pipeline stage a clean snapshot per cycle. ([[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits]]).
- [Register File](concepts/RegisterFile.md) — The array of [[CpuRegister|CPU registers]] inside the [[ProcessingUnit|processing unit]] — the **small, fast on-chip [[SRAM]] bank** the [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] reads operands from and writes results back to on every cycle of the [[FetchDecodeExecuteCycle|fetch-decode-execute cycle]]. [[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits|Ch 5.4.3]] **explicitly builds one register** (32 [[DLatch|D-latches]] sharing one `WE`) and **names but defers the multi-register file** — a [[Decoder|decoder]] on register-address bits gating each register's `WE` on writes, a [[Multiplexer|MUX]] selecting which register's outputs to read. Direct payoff of [[dis-5-4-2-control-circuits|Ch 5.4.2]]'s [[Decoder]] / [[Multiplexer|MUX]] / [[Demultiplexer|DMUX]] control circuits applied to the storage primitive. Architecturally visible — ISA names registers (`%rax` etc.) — and is the **fastest** tier of the [[MemoryHierarchy|memory hierarchy]]. ([[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits]] / [[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [DRAM](concepts/DRAM.md) — **Dynamic Random-Access Memory**. Each bit is stored as **charge on a tiny capacitor** addressed by a single pass transistor (1T1C cell). *"Dynamic RAM (DRAM) uses capacitors to store values and is slower but cheaper"* ([[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits|Ch 5.4.3]]). **Slower, denser, cheaper** than the circuit-based [[SRAM]] used for [[CpuRegister|registers]] / cache; charge leaks in milliseconds → controller must **refresh** rows periodically (~64ms). Populates the main-[[RAM|memory]] DIMMs of a typical computer; SRAM caches hide DRAM latency from the [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]]. Ch 5.4.3 introduces DRAM **only by name** — no 1T1C cell construction, no refresh circuitry, no DDR controller. ([[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits]]).

### Added with [[dis-5-4-2-control-circuits]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 5.4.2 Control Circuits)

- [Control Circuit](concepts/ControlCircuit.md) — Category-level page for the **second** of the three [[Circuit|circuit]] categories ([[dis-5-4-circuits|Ch 5.4]]'s partition). *"Control circuits are used throughout a system. On the processor, they drive the execution of program instructions on program data. They also control loading and storing values to different levels of storage (between registers, cache, and RAM)"* ([[dis-5-4-2-control-circuits|Ch 5.4.2]]). Where [[ArithmeticLogicCircuit|arithmetic-and-logic]] circuits *compute* and [[StorageCircuit|storage]] circuits *remember*, control circuits ***route*** — driven by select-bit signals from the [[ControlUnit|control unit]]'s decode phase. Three canonical examples: [[Multiplexer|MUX]], [[Demultiplexer|DMUX]], [[Decoder]]. **Promoted from forward-reference to category page.** ([[dis-5-4-2-control-circuits]]).
- [Multiplexer (MUX)](concepts/Multiplexer.md) — [[dis-5-4-2-control-circuits|Ch 5.4.2]]'s headline [[ControlCircuit|control circuit]]: *"a multiplexer (MUX) is an example of a control circuit that selects, or chooses, one of several values."* Two-way 1-bit form `Out = (NOT(S) AND B) OR (S AND A)` — two [[AndGate|AND]]s + one [[NotGate|NOT]] + one [[OrGate|OR]]. $N$-way generalizes to $\log_2 N$ select bits + $N$ AND gates + one $N$-way [[OrGate|OR]]; the select bits are decoded internally — *every MUX contains a [[Decoder|decoder]]*. Two-way $N$-bit MUX = $N$ parallel 1-bit MUXes on a shared select line. CPU role: *"the CPU may use a multiplexer circuit to select from which [[CpuRegister|CPU register]] to read an instruction operand value."* ([[dis-5-4-2-control-circuits]]).
- [Demultiplexer (DMUX)](concepts/Demultiplexer.md) — The [[Multiplexer|MUX]]'s dataflow inverse: *"a demultiplexer (DMUX) is the inverse of a multiplexer. Whereas a multiplexer chooses one of N inputs, a demultiplexer chooses one of N outputs"* ([[dis-5-4-2-control-circuits|Ch 5.4.2]]). 1 data input + $\log_2 N$ select bits → $N$ outputs (the selected one carries the input). Sits on the **write side** of the [[CpuRegister|register file]] and behind the [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] for result routing. ([[dis-5-4-2-control-circuits]]).
- [Decoder](concepts/Decoder.md) — [[ControlCircuit|Control circuit]] translating $N$ encoded input bits → $2^N$ one-hot output lines: *"a decoder circuit takes an encoded input and enables one of several outputs based on the input value"* ([[dis-5-4-2-control-circuits|Ch 5.4.2]]). Built from $2^N$ [[AndGate|AND]] gates each receiving the straight-or-inverted input combination matching its index. **Sits inside every $N$-way [[Multiplexer|MUX]]** as the internal select-bit translator. Also the *"decode"* in [[FetchDecodeExecuteCycle|fetch-decode-execute]] — the [[ControlUnit|control unit]] uses a decoder to translate [[InstructionRegister|IR]] opcode bits into operation-enable signals. **Encoder (inverse) is not introduced in Ch 5.4.2** — the word *"encoded"* refers to the input pattern only. ([[dis-5-4-2-control-circuits]]).

### Added with [[dis-5-4-1-arithmetic-logic-circuits]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 5.4.1 Arithmetic and Logic Circuits)

- [Arithmetic and Logic Circuit](concepts/ArithmeticLogicCircuit.md) — Category-level page for the **first** of the three [[Circuit|circuit]] categories ([[dis-5-4-circuits|Ch 5.4]]'s partition). Circuits that **operate on data** — arithmetic ([[HalfAdder|half adder]] / [[FullAdder|full adder]] / [[RippleCarryAdder|ripple-carry adder]] / subtraction wiring) and logic ([[OneBitEqualityCircuit|equality]] / M-bit gate networks). Codifies the **three-step methodology** ([[TruthTable|truth table]] → Boolean expression → [[LogicGate|gates]]) that recurs across the chapter. Promoted from forward-reference to category page. ([[dis-5-4-1-arithmetic-logic-circuits]]).
- [1-bit Equality Circuit](concepts/OneBitEqualityCircuit.md) — Combinational logic circuit, `1` iff `A == B`. *"(NOT(A) AND NOT(B)) OR (A AND B) — is 1 when A and B are both 0 or both 1"* ([[dis-5-4-1-arithmetic-logic-circuits|Ch 5.4.1]]) — equivalent to a single [[XnorGate|XNOR]] but built from the [[AndGate|AND]] / [[OrGate|OR]] / [[NotGate|NOT]] basis as a methodology demonstration. M-bit equality stacks M of these AND-ed together. ([[dis-5-4-1-arithmetic-logic-circuits]]).
- [Half Adder](concepts/HalfAdder.md) — The minimal arithmetic circuit: two 1-bit inputs (`A`, `B`), two outputs (`Sum = A XOR B`; `CarryOut = A AND B`). One [[XorGate|XOR]] + one [[AndGate|AND]]. Called *"1-bit adder"* in Ch 5.4.1; **"half" because it has no `CarryIn`** — a [[FullAdder|full adder]] adds that. ([[dis-5-4-1-arithmetic-logic-circuits]]).
- [Full Adder](concepts/FullAdder.md) — Three-input adder (`A`, `B`, `CarryIn`) → two outputs (`Sum = A XOR B XOR CarryIn`, `CarryOut = majority(A, B, CarryIn)`). The 8-row truth table [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]] introduced at the bit-pattern level now gets its **gate-level construction** (two [[HalfAdder|half adders]] + one [[OrGate|OR]]). The per-bit primitive of multi-bit addition. **Promoted from cross-chapter forward-reference stub** to first-class page. ([[dis-5-4-1-arithmetic-logic-circuits]] / [[dis-4-4-1-addition]]).
- [Ripple-Carry Adder](concepts/RippleCarryAdder.md) — Ch 5.4.1's headline N-bit construction: $N$ [[FullAdder|full adders]] cascaded by carry (`CarryOut[i] → CarryIn[i+1]`). *"This type of N-bit adder circuit, built from N 1-bit adder circuits, is called a ripple carry adder"* — *"the SUM result ripples or propagates through the circuit from the low-order to the high-order bits."* Doubles as subtractor with inverters on `B` + `CarryIn_0 = 1` (gate-level realization of [[dis-4-4-2-subtraction|Ch 4.4.2]]'s flip-and-add-one). Worst-case propagation $\Theta(N)$ gate delays — the latency real CPUs optimize via carry-lookahead (out of scope). ([[dis-5-4-1-arithmetic-logic-circuits]]).

### Added with [[dis-5-4-circuits]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 5.4 Circuits)

- [Digital Circuit](concepts/Circuit.md) — Umbrella concept for a composition of [[LogicGate|gates]] and wires implementing a Boolean function (combinational) or a stateful component (sequential). *"Digital circuits implement the core functionality of the [[VonNeumannArchitecture|architecture]]"* ([[dis-5-4-circuits|Ch 5.4]]). Design discipline = **hierarchical composition + black-box [[Abstraction|abstraction]]**. Three categories partition processor circuitry: [[ArithmeticLogicCircuit|arithmetic & logic]] (Ch 5.4.1), [[ControlCircuit|control]] (Ch 5.4.2), [[StorageCircuit|storage]] (Ch 5.4.3). ([[dis-5-4-circuits]]).

### Added with [[dis-5-3-gates]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 5.3 Logic Gates)

- [Logic Gate](concepts/LogicGate.md) — The elementary digital-circuit primitive: a small [[Transistor|transistor]] circuit computing one [[BooleanAlgebra|Boolean]] operation over 1-bit inputs. *"The building blocks of the digital circuitry that implements arithmetic, control, and storage"* ([[dis-5-3-gates|Ch 5.3]]). Umbrella over the seven canonical gates. ([[dis-5-3-gates]]).
- [AND Gate](concepts/AndGate.md) — Two-input gate; output `1` iff both inputs are `1` (`A·B`). Member of the functionally-complete basis {AND, OR, NOT}. Used for **bit masking** and in the [[FullAdder|full-adder]]'s `CarryOut` generation. ([[dis-5-3-gates]]).
- [OR Gate](concepts/OrGate.md) — Two-input gate; output `1` iff at least one input is `1` (`A+B`). Member of the functionally-complete basis. Used for **bit setting** and to combine [[FullAdder|full-adder]] carry contributions. ([[dis-5-3-gates]]).
- [NOT Gate (Inverter)](concepts/NotGate.md) — The unique single-input gate; outputs the inverse of its input. The negation primitive — combined with [[AndGate|AND]] / [[OrGate|OR]] it produces the derived gates. ([[dis-5-3-gates]]).
- [NAND Gate](concepts/NandGate.md) — Negation of [[AndGate|AND]] (`¬(A·B)`). **Functionally complete on its own** — any digital circuit can be built from NANDs alone (the universality CMOS layouts exploit). ([[dis-5-3-gates]]).
- [NOR Gate](concepts/NorGate.md) — Negation of [[OrGate|OR]] (`¬(A+B)`). *"(A NOR B) ≡ NOT(A OR B)"* ([[dis-5-3-gates|Ch 5.3]]). Also functionally complete on its own; the Apollo Guidance Computer was built entirely from 3-input NORs. ([[dis-5-3-gates]]).
- [XOR Gate](concepts/XorGate.md) — Two-input gate; output `1` iff inputs *differ* (`A⊕B`). **The headline gate for [[BinaryArithmetic|binary arithmetic]]** — `Sum = A XOR B XOR CarryIn` in the [[FullAdder|full-adder]] ([[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]]); also the mode-controlled invert in [[dis-4-4-2-subtraction|Ch 4.4.2]]'s subtraction trick. Self-inverse `(x ^ k) ^ k = x`. ([[dis-5-3-gates]]).
- [XNOR Gate](concepts/XnorGate.md) — Negation of [[XorGate|XOR]]; output `1` iff inputs are *equal*. Used in **equality comparators** — bitwise XNOR + M-input AND tests whether two M-bit words match. ([[dis-5-3-gates]]).
- [Truth Table](concepts/TruthTable.md) — Exhaustive $2^N$-row enumeration of every input combination → output mapping; the canonical specification format for combinational circuits. Examples: the four-row tables for each gate; the **8-row [[FullAdder|full-adder]] table** of [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]] (`Sum = XOR`, `CarryOut = majority`). ([[dis-5-3-gates]] / [[dis-4-4-1-addition]]).
- [Transistor](concepts/Transistor.md) — Semiconductor **voltage-controlled switch** — *"can switch its state between on or off (between a high or low voltage output)"* ([[dis-5-3-gates|Ch 5.3]]). The physical primitive beneath every [[LogicGate|logic gate]]; modern CPUs pack $>10^{10}$ on a die. The substrate one level below the gate abstraction. ([[dis-5-3-gates]]).

### Added with [[dis-5-2-von-neumann]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 5.2 The von Neumann Architecture)

- [Control Unit](concepts/ControlUnit.md) — The half of the [[CPU]] that **drives instruction execution** — fetches the next instruction from [[RAM|memory]], decodes its opcode and operand specifiers, dispatches to the [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]], and writes the result back. Owns the [[ProgramCounter|program counter (PC)]] (address of next instruction) and [[InstructionRegister|instruction register (IR)]] (currently-decoding instruction). Together with the [[ProcessingUnit|processing unit]] it forms the [[CPU]]. ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [Arithmetic / Logic Unit (ALU)](concepts/ArithmeticLogicUnit.md) — The part of the [[ProcessingUnit|processing unit]] that **performs the actual computation** — arithmetic (+/−/×/÷), [[BooleanAlgebra|boolean]] / logical operations, comparisons. The active element of the [[FetchDecodeExecuteCycle|fetch-decode-execute cycle]]'s *execute* phase. Where the [[ControlUnit|control unit]] decides *what* and *when*, the ALU is *how*. Promoted from forward-reference stub. ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [Processing Unit](concepts/ProcessingUnit.md) — The **data-path half** of the [[CPU]] — comprises the [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] and the [[CpuRegister|register file]]. Together with the [[ControlUnit|control unit]] (the sequencing half) it forms the [[CPU]]. Each [[CpuRegister|register]] holds one [[DataWord|data word]]. ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [Bus (System Bus)](concepts/Bus.md) — A *"communication channel that transfers binary values between communication endpoints"* ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann|Ch 5.2]]). Three classical buses split the wires by what kind of value travels: [[ControlBus|control bus]] (commands), [[AddressBus|address bus]] (memory addresses), [[DataBus|data bus]] (the actual bytes). Splitting enables parallel traffic — the throughput limit when shared is the [[VonNeumannBottleneck|von Neumann bottleneck]]. ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [Control Bus](concepts/ControlBus.md) — One of three classical [[Bus|system buses]]; carries **command and control signals** (read vs write, interrupts, bus-grant, clock, ready/busy) between [[CPU]], [[RAM|memory]], and [[IODevice|I/O devices]]. The *how / when* sibling to [[AddressBus|address bus]]'s *where* and [[DataBus|data bus]]'s *what*. ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [Address Bus](concepts/AddressBus.md) — One of three classical [[Bus|system buses]]; carries the **[[RAM|memory]] address** for the current read/write request. **Width caps addressable [[RAM|RAM]]**: 32-bit → $2^{32}$ bytes = **4 GiB** ceiling (the historical 32-bit OS limit); 64-bit → 16 EiB (only 48–57 bits wired in practice). ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [Data Bus](concepts/DataBus.md) — One of three classical [[Bus|system buses]]; carries the **actual byte / word values** being read from or written to [[RAM|memory]] or [[IODevice|I/O]]. Typically [[DataWord|word]]-width; modern systems decouple internal word size from external memory-channel width. ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [I/O Device](concepts/IODevice.md) — Peripheral that crosses the boundary between the computer and the outside world — bringing external data in ([[InputDevice|input]]) or relaying results out ([[OutputDevice|output]]); some devices (touchscreens, storage drives, NICs) are bidirectional. The fourth and fifth of the [[VonNeumannArchitecture|von Neumann architecture]]'s five functional units. ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [Input Device](concepts/InputDevice.md) — Peripheral that **brings external data and instructions into the computer** — keyboard, mouse, camera, microphone, scanner. One of the five functional units; the headline mechanism that makes the [[StoredProgram|stored-program]] principle useful in practice (programs *load* via input rather than rewiring). ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [Output Device](concepts/OutputDevice.md) — Peripheral that **stores or displays the computer's results** — monitor, speakers, printer, haptic actuators. One of the five functional units; the result-delivery side of [[IODevice|I/O]]. ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [Fetch-Decode-Execute Cycle](concepts/FetchDecodeExecuteCycle.md) — The *operational heart* of the [[VonNeumannArchitecture|von Neumann architecture]]: the repeating four-phase loop **fetch** (read instruction at [[ProgramCounter|PC]] into [[InstructionRegister|IR]]; increment PC) → **decode** ([[ControlUnit|control unit]] parses opcode + operand locations) → **execute** ([[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] performs operation) → **store** (write result back via [[DataBus|data]] / [[AddressBus|address]] / [[ControlBus|control]] buses). Because *every* instruction runs the same four phases, the same hardware can run any [[StoredProgram|stored program]]. ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [Program Counter (PC)](concepts/ProgramCounter.md) — Special [[CpuRegister|register]] inside the [[ControlUnit|control unit]] holding the **[[RAM|memory]] address of the *next* instruction to execute**. The single piece of state that makes the [[FetchDecodeExecuteCycle|fetch-decode-execute cycle]] sequential. Architectural surface: `%eip` / `%rip` on x86 / x86-64, `pc` / `r15` on ARM, `pc` on RISC-V. ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [Instruction Register (IR)](concepts/InstructionRegister.md) — Special [[CpuRegister|register]] inside the [[ControlUnit|control unit]] holding the **currently-decoding instruction word** — the bit pattern fetched from [[RAM|memory]] at the address that was in the [[ProgramCounter|PC]]. Not user-visible on most ISAs — an internal pipeline buffer the [[ControlUnit|control unit]]'s decode logic reads. ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [Byte-Addressable Memory](concepts/ByteAddressable.md) — The addressing convention where **each [[RAM|memory]] address corresponds to exactly one byte** — the unit of addressing equals the unit of access granularity. Makes the [[AddressBus|address-bus-width]] ↔ addressable-byte exponent identity one-to-one. The C / strings / byte-level I/O ecosystem requires it (the historical word-addressable alternative is extinct outside DSPs). ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).
- [Data Word](concepts/DataWord.md) — The **natural unit of data** a [[CPU]] manipulates — the size of one [[CpuRegister|register]], the width of the [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] data path, and (typically) the width of the [[DataBus|data bus]]. Per [[dis-5-2-von-neumann|Ch 5.2]] *"each register stores one data word."* The headline architectural parameter — *"32-bit"* / *"64-bit"* labels refer to word size. ([[dis-5-2-von-neumann]]).

### Added with [[dis-5-1-history]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 5.1 The Origins of Modern Computing)

- [Alan Turing](entities/AlanTuring.md) — British mathematician (1912–1954); proposed the [[TuringMachine|abstract Logical Computing Machine]] (1937) that defines computability, led the [[BletchleyPark]] Enigma cryptanalysis effort during WWII. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [John von Neumann](entities/JohnVonNeumann.md) — Hungarian-American mathematician; authored the *First Draft of a Report on the [[EDVAC]]* (1945) describing what became the [[VonNeumannArchitecture|von Neumann architecture]] — the **instructions-and-data-in-the-same-memory** synthesis underlying essentially every modern computer. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [Charles Babbage](entities/CharlesBabbage.md) — 19th-century English mathematician; designed the [[AnalyticalEngine]] (1837) — the conceptual ancestor of programmable computers, never fully built. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [Ada Lovelace](entities/AdaLovelace.md) — 19th-century English mathematician; wrote the first algorithm intended for execution on [[CharlesBabbage|Babbage]]'s [[AnalyticalEngine]] — historically recognized as the **first computer programmer**. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [Konrad Zuse](entities/KonradZuse.md) — German engineer; built the [[Z3]] (1941), the **first programmable electromechanical binary computer**, in wartime isolation from the Anglo-American tradition. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [Tommy Flowers](entities/TommyFlowers.md) — British Post Office engineer; built [[Colossus]] (1943) for [[BletchleyPark]] — the first programmable electronic digital computer, classified for decades. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [Howard Aiken](entities/HowardAiken.md) — Harvard physicist; led the design of the [[HarvardMarkI]] (1944), an electromechanical paper-tape-programmed calculator used for [[ManhattanProject|Manhattan Project]] calculations. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [John Mauchly](entities/JohnMauchly.md) — Co-designer of [[ENIAC]] (1945) at the [[UniversityOfPennsylvania|University of Pennsylvania]] with [[PresperEckert]]; later co-founded the first commercial computer company. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [J. Presper Eckert](entities/PresperEckert.md) — Co-designer of [[ENIAC]] (1945) with [[JohnMauchly]]; the engineering counterpart to Mauchly's design vision. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [Grace Hopper](entities/GraceHopper.md) — U.S. Navy mathematician; programmed the [[HarvardMarkI]], pioneered compiler technology and the COBOL programming language. One of the women whose contributions Ch 5.1 explicitly foregrounds against historical underrecognition. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [Turing Machine](concepts/TuringMachine.md) — [[AlanTuring|Turing]]'s 1937 abstract model of computation: a tape, a read-write head, and a finite state machine. Defines what is *computable* independent of any physical implementation; underlies the [[ChurchTuringThesis|Church-Turing thesis]] and the formal notion of an **algorithm**. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [Von Neumann Architecture](concepts/VonNeumannArchitecture.md) — The **stored-program** architecture: instructions and data share the same internal memory, with a single CPU fetching and executing both. The structural thesis of Ch 5; named for the [[EDVAC]] paper's organizing principle. Underlies essentially every modern general-purpose computer. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [Stored Program](concepts/StoredProgram.md) — The architectural principle that **executable instructions are stored in the same writable memory as data** — the defining property of the [[VonNeumannArchitecture]]. Contrasts with patch-cable / paper-tape configurations of earlier machines like [[ENIAC]] (which had to be physically rewired to change programs). ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [Z3 (Computer)](concepts/Z3.md) — [[KonradZuse|Zuse]]'s 1941 electromechanical binary computer in Germany — the **first programmable** computer, using relays and reading programs from punched film. Built in wartime isolation; survived the war on paper after the physical machine was destroyed. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [Colossus](concepts/Colossus.md) — The [[TommyFlowers|Flowers]]-designed 1943 cryptanalysis computer at [[BletchleyPark]], used to break German Lorenz cipher traffic. Operated by the [[WomensRoyalNavalService|Women's Royal Naval Service (WRNS)]]. Its existence was classified for decades after the war. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [Harvard Architecture](concepts/HarvardArchitecture.md) — CPU architecture with separate program and data memories on separate buses; enables next-instruction fetch in parallel with data load. The model used by [[AVR]] / [[ATmega328P]] and (in modified form) [[ARMCortexM|ARM Cortex-M]]. Opposite: [[VonNeumannArchitecture]] ([[embedded-controllers-fiore]] ch. 2 / 16).
- [Harvard Mark I](concepts/HarvardMarkI.md) — [[HowardAiken|Aiken]]'s 1944 electromechanical Harvard calculator; programmed via paper tape; ran calculations for the [[ManhattanProject|atomic-bomb]] project; programmed by [[GraceHopper]]. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [ENIAC](concepts/ENIAC.md) — [[JohnMauchly|Mauchly]] / [[PresperEckert|Eckert]]'s 1945 fully-electronic decimal computer at the [[UniversityOfPennsylvania|University of Pennsylvania]] — *"the first programmable, electronic, general-purpose digital computer."* Programmed by **six women** (Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas, Ruth Lichterman) whose contributions were historically uncredited. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [EDVAC](concepts/EDVAC.md) — [[JohnVonNeumann|von Neumann]]'s 1945 *First Draft of a Report* — the unifying synthesis describing what became the [[VonNeumannArchitecture]]: a single internal memory holding both instructions and data, accessed by a CPU. The structural thesis Ch 5.2+ operationalizes. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).
- [Analytical Engine](concepts/AnalyticalEngine.md) — [[CharlesBabbage|Babbage]]'s 1837 design for a mechanical, programmable general-purpose computer — the conceptual ancestor of modern computers, never fully constructed in his lifetime. The machine [[AdaLovelace|Lovelace]] wrote the first algorithm for. ([[dis-5-1-history]]).

### Added with [[dis-4-8-floating-point]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 4.8 Real Numbers in Binary)

- [Floating Point](concepts/FloatingPoint.md) — Binary encoding of real numbers where the **binary point moves** with the value (unlike [[FixedPoint|fixed-point]]'s pinned point), decoded as $(-1)^{\text{sign}} \cdot 1.\text{mantissa} \cdot 2^{\text{exponent} - \text{bias}}$. Three fields: [[SignBit|sign]] / [[Exponent|exponent]] / [[Mantissa|significand]]. Gives **uniform relative precision** (~7 decimal digits in `binary32`) over an enormous dynamic range ($\sim 10^{\pm 38}$ for 32-bit). [[dis-4-8-floating-point|Ch 4.8]]'s opening claim: *"for any binary encoding of real numbers, there exist values that cannot be represented exactly."* Standardized by [[IEEE754|IEEE 754]]. Shares the **non-associative-under-rounding** arithmetic property with [[FixedPoint|fixed-point]] — *"like fixed-point, rounding problems similarly affect floating-point encodings."* See [[FloatingPointPrecision]] for rounding-error consequences. ([[dis-4-8-floating-point]]).
- [IEEE 754](concepts/IEEE754.md) — IEEE Standard for Floating-Point Arithmetic (1985, revised 2008 / 2019) — the dominant [[FloatingPoint|floating-point]] format on every modern [[CPU]] / [[GPU]] / language runtime. *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* [[dis-4-8-floating-point|Ch 4.8]] covers only the **32-bit `binary32`** subset: 1-bit [[SignBit|sign]] / 8-bit [[Exponent|exponent]] (bias 127) / 23-bit [[Mantissa|significand]] (implicit leading 1). Worked example: `0b11000001101101000000000000000000 = -22.5` (sign `1`, exponent field 131 → factor $2^4 = 16$, significand $1.40625$). Wiki-only deepenings: `binary64` (52-bit mantissa, bias 1023, ~15 decimal digits); `binary16` half / `bfloat16` (ML); denormalized / $\pm 0$ / $\pm \infty$ / `NaN` special encodings (exponent = all-zeros or all-ones); five rounding modes (default: round-to-nearest-even). ([[dis-4-8-floating-point]]).
- [Mantissa (Significand)](concepts/Mantissa.md) — The **fractional-precision field** of a [[FloatingPoint|floating-point]] number — carries the value's significant digits while [[Exponent|exponent]] carries the scale. In [[IEEE754|IEEE 754]] `binary32`: 23 stored bits + 1 implicit leading 1 (normalization rule) = 24 bits of precision, giving relative precision $\epsilon = 2^{-23} \approx 1.19 \times 10^{-7}$ (machine epsilon — name not in chapter) and ~7.22 significant decimal digits. [[dis-4-8-floating-point|Ch 4.8]]: *"the fractional portion behaves like the fixed-point representation"* — each bit $f_i$ contributes $2^{i-23}$, exactly the negative-power-of-2 place-value scheme of [[FixedPoint|fixed-point]]. Stored field `10110100…0` → significand $1.40625$ (the $-22.5$ worked example). In `binary64`: 52 + 1 = 53 bits → ~15–17 decimal digits, $\epsilon \approx 2.22 \times 10^{-16}$. ([[dis-4-8-floating-point]]).
- [Exponent (Floating-Point)](concepts/Exponent.md) — The **scaling field** of a [[FloatingPoint|floating-point]] number — determines the power of 2 by which the [[Mantissa|significand]] is multiplied. [[IEEE754|IEEE 754]] `binary32` uses **8 bits, bias 127** — *"the significand gets multiplied by $2^{\text{exponent} - 127}$, where the 127 is a bias"* ([[dis-4-8-floating-point|Ch 4.8]]). Why a bias not a sign bit? Avoids stealing a bit for sign; gives lexicographic-bit-pattern ordering matching numerical ordering (lets hardware comparators reuse the integer-compare circuit on positive floats). Bias = $2^{k-1} - 1$ for $k$-bit exponent — 127 for `binary32`, 1023 for `binary64` (11-bit), 15 for `binary16` (5-bit). `binary32` normal range $E_{\text{true}} \in [-126, +127]$, dynamic range $\sim 10^{\pm 38}$. Reserved encodings: $E_{\text{stored}} = 0$ (subnormal / $\pm 0$) and $E_{\text{stored}} = 255$ ($\pm \infty$ / NaN). ([[dis-4-8-floating-point]]).
- [Fixed Point](concepts/FixedPoint.md) — Binary encoding of real numbers extending [[UnsignedInteger|unsigned-integer]] place-value to **negative powers of 2** at a **predetermined, pinned [[BinaryPoint|binary point]]** position — *"bits left of the point use positive powers; bits right use $2^{-1}, 2^{-2}, \ldots$"* ([[dis-4-8-floating-point|Ch 4.8]]). Worked example: `0b000101.10` = $4 + 1 + 0.5 = 5.5$. With $N$ fractional bits, smallest gap is $2^{-N}$ — **uniform absolute precision**, the foil to [[FloatingPoint|floating-point]]'s relative precision. **Rounding non-associativity** demonstration: $(0.75 / 2) \cdot 3 = 0.75$ (divide rounds $0.375 \to 0.25$); $(0.75 \cdot 3) / 2 = 1.00$ (multiply produces $2.25$ which rounds to $2.00$); exact answer $1.125$ in both cases — *"operation order matters under rounding."* Wins over [[FloatingPoint|float]] in: embedded / DSP / [[FPGA|FPGAs]] (no FPU silicon), audio sample chains (bounded dynamic range), financial code (use 64-bit cents — `0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3` in `binary64`). Q-format conventions (`Q15`, `Q31`) dominate DSP. ([[dis-4-8-floating-point]]).
- [Floating-Point Precision (Rounding Error)](concepts/FloatingPointPrecision.md) — The bounded-precision property of [[IEEE754|IEEE 754]] [[FloatingPoint|float]] arithmetic — relative precision $\epsilon \approx 2^{-23} \approx 1.19 \times 10^{-7}$ for `binary32`, $\epsilon \approx 2.22 \times 10^{-16}$ for `binary64`. [[dis-4-8-floating-point|Ch 4.8]]'s shared-pathology claim: *"like fixed-point, rounding problems similarly affect floating-point encodings."* **Non-associativity** under rounding — $(a \cdot b) \cdot c \ne a \cdot (b \cdot c)$ in general — produces failure modes: **catastrophic cancellation** (subtracting nearly-equal values), **accumulated rounding** (naïve $N$-sum loses $\sim \log_2 N$ bits — [[KahanSummation|Kahan summation]] recovers), **cross-precision conversion** (lossy / overflowing). Two cited real-world catastrophes: **1991 Patriot** missile system in Dhahran ($0.1 \cdot$ time-counter accumulated drift over 100+ hours → Scud miss → 28 dead U.S. soldiers; fix existed, not installed); **1996 Ariane 5** explosion 39 seconds post-launch (64-bit-float velocity → 16-bit-signed-int conversion overflowed — the [[dis-4-5-overflow|Ch 4.5]] mechanism at the float-to-int boundary — unhandled exception cascade → self-destruct). Defenses (wiki, not chapter): use `decimal` for money / integers for counts / [[FixedPoint|fixed-point]] for bounded-domain DSP; compare with tolerance not equality; numerically stable algorithms; saturating/checked conversion; disable `-ffast-math` for reproducibility. ([[dis-4-8-floating-point]]).

### Added with [[dis-4-7-byte-order]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 4.7 Integer Byte Order)

- [Byte Order](concepts/ByteOrder.md) — **Umbrella concept page** for the byte-layout convention also called [[Endianness|endianness]]: *"byte order, sometimes referred to as endianness, describes the order in which the bytes of a multibyte value are ordered in memory"* ([[dis-4-7-byte-order|Ch 4.7]]). A property of the [[CPU]] / [[InstructionSetArchitecture|ISA]] — not of the language or program — observable whenever bytes cross a machine / file / wire boundary. **Two conventions**: [[BigEndian|big-endian]] (MSByte at lowest address — matches written numerals) and [[LittleEndian|little-endian]] (LSByte at lowest address — reversed). Single-byte values have no endianness. **Detection** via `char *` cast: `int v = 0xAABBCCDD; char *p = (char *) &v;` walking `p[0..3]` reveals the host's order (x86 prints `DD CC BB AA`). **Conversion** via [[POSIX]] `htonl` / `ntohl` / `htons` / `ntohs`, GCC `__builtin_bswap{16,32,64}`, x86 [[BSWAP|`bswap`]] (single-cycle since 80486), ARM `REV` / `REV16`. Three canonical leak scenarios: network transmission, file formats, debugger raw-memory inspection. ([[dis-4-7-byte-order]]).
- [Endianness](concepts/Endianness.md) — Alias term for [[ByteOrder|byte order]], more common in source code (`__BYTE_ORDER__`, `<endian.h>`, Rust `to_le` / `to_be`, Python `struct.pack(">i", x)`) while *byte order* dominates in textbooks. Same two values: [[BigEndian|big-endian]] (network protocols, [[PowerPC]], [[SPARC]]) and [[LittleEndian|little-endian]] ([[X86]] / [[ARM]] / [[RISCV|RISC-V]] — virtually all deployed CPUs in 2025). Etymology from Jonathan Swift's *[[GulliversTravels|Gulliver's Travels]]* (1726) via [[DannyCohen|Danny Cohen]]'s 1980 [[IETF]] IEN-137 memo *On Holy Wars and a Plea for Peace*. ([[dis-4-7-byte-order]]).
- [Big-Endian](concepts/BigEndian.md) — The [[ByteOrder|byte-order]] convention where the **most significant byte** occupies the **lowest** memory address; subsequent bytes follow in **descending** significance. For `0xAABBCCDD` at `p`: bytes walk `AA BB CC DD` across `p, p+1, p+2, p+3` — same left-to-right order as the written numeral. **Where used**: [[NetworkByteOrder|network byte order]] (the [[IETF]]-mandated standard — *"the IETF defines big-endian as the network byte order"*), [[PowerPC]] (default), [[SPARC]], [[Motorola68k]] (classic Mac / Amiga / Atari ST), [[IBM360]] / [[IBMZArchitecture|z/Architecture]] mainframes, [[JavaVirtualMachine|JVM]] bytecode layout, [[JPEG]] / [[TIFF]] (MM mode) / [[PNG]] chunk headers. **Practical implications**: `gdb`'s `x/4xb` output matches the value's hex literal directly (no mental reversal); `htonl(x) == x` (no-op); `memcmp` preserves numeric ordering. **Decline**: rare in deployed CPUs as of 2025 — last major holdouts are [[IBMZArchitecture|IBM z/Architecture]] mainframes and network-protocol code paths. ([[dis-4-7-byte-order]]).
- [Little-Endian](concepts/LittleEndian.md) — The [[ByteOrder|byte-order]] convention where the **least significant byte** occupies the **lowest** memory address; subsequent bytes follow in **ascending** significance. For `0xAABBCCDD` at `p`: bytes walk `DD CC BB AA` across `p, p+1, p+2, p+3` — **reversed** from the written numeral. **Where used (dominant in 2025)**: [[X86]] / [[X86_64]] (universal since [[Intel8080]] 1974), [[ARM]] / [[AArch64]] (default — bi-endian capability dormant on [[Linux]] / [[iOS]] / [[Android]] / [[Windows]]), [[RISCV|RISC-V]] (default), [[Alpha]], [[POWER8]]+ on Linux, most modern binary formats ([[BMP]], [[WAV]] / [[RIFF]], [[PE|PE/COFF]] Windows executables, [[ELF]] on x86 / ARM targets, [[ZIP]]). **Why it persists despite visual confusion**: address-of-low-byte == address-of-value (truncating casts are no-ops); increment-with-carry flows naturally from low to high; multiprecision arithmetic mirrors single-precision. **Practical implications**: `gdb`'s `x/4xb` shows reversed bytes — perennial source of beginner confusion; `htonl` / `ntohl` are real byte-swap operations (not no-ops); `memcmp` is **unrelated** to numeric ordering of integers. **#1 cross-platform networking bug**: forgetting `htonl` on little-endian hosts. ([[dis-4-7-byte-order]]).

### Added with [[dis-4-6-bitwise]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 4.6 Bitwise Operators)

- [Bitwise Operator](concepts/BitwiseOperator.md) — Umbrella for the four bit-level boolean operators [[CLanguage|C]] exposes: [[BitwiseAnd|AND `&`]] (per-bit AND — `26 & 54 = 18`; masking), [[BitwiseOr|OR `|`]] (per-bit OR — `26 | 54 = 62`; bit-setting), [[BitwiseXor|XOR `^`]] (per-bit XOR — `26 ^ 54 = 44`; toggling / equality-test via `a ^ b == 0`), and [[BitwiseNot|NOT `~`]] (unary bit-flip — `~26 = -27` under [[TwosComplement|two's complement]] since *"bitwise NOT only flips the bits and doesn't add one"* — hence `~x = -x - 1`). Per [[dis-4-6-bitwise|Ch 4.6]] *"bitwise operators directly apply logic gate behavior to bit sequences"* — they instantiate [[LogicGate|AND / OR / XOR / NOT]] gates per bit position, execute in one clock cycle with no carry propagation, and are the cheapest ops in the [[InstructionSetArchitecture|ISA]]. Distinguished from the [[LogicalOperator|logical operators]] (`&&` / `||` / `!`) which short-circuit on truth values — the chapter's headline category warning. Canonical idioms: bit-test `x & (1<<i)`, set `x |= (1<<i)`, clear `x &= ~(1<<i)`, toggle `x ^= (1<<i)`, field-mask `(x >> shift) & ((1<<width) - 1)`, power-of-two test `(x & (x-1)) == 0`. Maps to x86 `AND` / `OR` / `XOR` / `NOT` and ARM `AND` / `ORR` / `EOR` / `MVN`. ([[dis-4-6-bitwise]]).
- [Bit Shift](concepts/BitShift.md) — The `<<` / `>>` operator family that moves all bits in an $N$-bit value left or right by some number of positions, discarding bits that fall off one end and filling the vacated positions on the other. Per [[dis-4-6-bitwise|Ch 4.6]], **left shift `<<`** zero-fills from the right and truncates at the [[MostSignificantBit|MSB]] — `13 << 3 = 104` (`0b00001101 << 3 = 0b01101000`); **effect = multiplication by $2^N$** (the [[dis-4-4-3-mult-div|Ch 4.4.3]]-deferred *bit-shift power-of-two shortcut* finally delivered). **Right shift `>>` splits into two variants by operand type**: [[LogicalRightShift|logical right shift]] (unsigned operands → zero-fill — `0xFF000000 >> 12 = 0x000FF000`; effect = floor division by $2^N$) and [[ArithmeticRightShift|arithmetic right shift]] (signed operands → replicate [[SignBit|sign bit]] — `0xFF000000 >> 12 = 0xFFFFF000`; preserves sign of negative [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] values). *"The C compiler automatically selects the appropriate shifting variant based on variable declaration."* Arithmetic right shift floor-divides (rounds toward $-\infty$); disagrees with [[CLanguage|C]] `/` operator on negative dividends (which truncates toward zero — `(-1) >> 1 == -1` but `(-1) / 2 == 0`). **[[UndefinedBehavior|UB]] pitfalls** (wiki-only, not in chapter): shift by `>=` operand width is UB; negative shift count is UB; signed left-shift past the sign bit is UB; compilers strength-reduce `x * 8` to `shl 3` automatically. Hardware: single-cycle via barrel shifter (`SHL` / `SHR` / `SAR` on x86; `LSL` / `LSR` / `ASR` on ARM); ARM embeds free shifts in the second operand of data-processing instructions (`ADD r0, r1, r2, LSL #3`). ([[dis-4-6-bitwise]], [[dis-4-4-3-mult-div]]).

### Added with [[dis-4-5-overflow]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 4.5 Overflow)

- [Integer Overflow](concepts/IntegerOverflow.md) — The condition where the mathematical result of an integer operation exceeds the fixed-width storage holding it — *"a computation that lacks the storage to represent its result has **overflowed**"* ([[dis-4-5-overflow|Ch 4.5]]). All N-bit integer arithmetic is **modular** ($\text{result} \equiv \text{true} \pmod{2^N}$); whether the bit pattern counts as overflow depends on the encoding. **Unsigned rule**: *"the carry out must match the carry in, otherwise the operation causes overflow"* — MSB [[CarryOut|carry-out]] in addition = overflow, absent expected carry-out in subtraction = overflow (resolves [[dis-4-4-2-subtraction|Ch 4.4.2]]'s deferred caveat). **[[TwosComplement|Two's-complement]] rule**: same-sign operands producing a different-sign result indicates overflow; mixed-sign addition can never overflow. The **same adder** produces both `CF` (unsigned) and `OF` (signed) flag signals — software / [[CCompiler|the compiler]] chooses which to read. Distinct from [[BufferOverflow|buffer overflow]] despite the shared word. Real-world cases: YouTube's 32-bit Gangnam Style counter (2014), Pac-Man's level-256 kill screen (1980), Therac-25 safety-flag overflow (1980s). ([[dis-4-5-overflow]]).
- [Undefined Behavior (C / C++)](concepts/UndefinedBehavior.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] / C++ standard category for constructs whose effect is deliberately unconstrained — *anything may happen*. Distinct from *implementation-defined* (must be documented) and *unspecified* (compiler picks from a finite set). The optimization licence the standard grants: *"if a path would invoke UB, the compiler may assume that path is never taken"* — and may prune it accordingly. Canonical case introduced by [[dis-4-5-overflow|Ch 4.5]]: **signed [[IntegerOverflow|integer overflow]] is UB** (compilers may delete `if (x + 1 < x)` for signed `x` because the predicate could only be true under UB), while **unsigned overflow is defined modular wrap**. Other major UB categories: out-of-bounds array access, [[NullPointer|null]]-deref, [[UseAfterFree|UAF]], data races, strict-aliasing violations, uninitialized reads, missing `return`, `INT_MIN / -1`. Mitigations: [[Valgrind]] / [[AddressSanitizer]] (subset coverage), UBSan (`-fsanitize=undefined`), `-fwrapv` (forfeits the licence), [[MISRA_C|MISRA-C]] / [[CERT_C|CERT-C]] coding standards (prohibits UB-prone constructs in safety-critical code). ([[dis-4-5-overflow]]).

### Added with [[dis-4-4-3-mult-div]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 4.4.3 Multiplication and Division)

- [Binary Multiplication](concepts/BinaryMultiplication.md) — The base-$2$ instantiation of pencil-and-paper **long multiplication** — *the decimal long-multiplication algorithm transferred to base 2 with only the base changing from $10$ to $2$*. Per [[dis-4-4-3-mult-div|Ch 4.4.3]], each multiplier bit produces a partial-product row that is **either the multiplicand itself (bit = 1) or zero (bit = 0)** — binary's digit alphabet $\{0,1\}$ eliminates decimal's $9 \times 9$ multiplication-table requirement, reducing the operation to *select-or-zero, shift, and add*. Each row is **shifted left** by its bit position ($d_0$ no shift, $d_1$ shift 1, etc.); the final result is the sum of all rows computed via [[BinaryAddition|Ch 4.4.1 binary addition]]. Worked example $\mathtt{0b0101} \times \mathtt{0b0011}$ (5 × 3): $\mathtt{0b0101}$ + $\mathtt{0b1010}$ = $\mathtt{0b1111}$ (15). Hardware multipliers (Booth's algorithm / Wallace trees) and the [[BitShift|bit-shift]] power-of-two shortcut are **explicitly out of scope** — Ch 4.4.3's disclaimer *"these methods do not reflect the behavior of modern hardware and are not meant to be comprehensive"* applies. ([[dis-4-4-3-mult-div]]).
- [Binary Division](concepts/BinaryDivision.md) — The base-$2$ instantiation of pencil-and-paper **long division** — *grade-school long division transferred to base 2 with only the base changing from $10$ to $2$*. Per [[dis-4-4-3-mult-div|Ch 4.4.3]], at each step the running remainder $R$ shifts left and the next dividend bit shifts in; the "how many times does the divisor fit?" decision reduces to a **single magnitude comparison** $R \ge B$ — quotient bit `1` and subtract, or quotient bit `0` and skip — eliminating decimal's $0$–$9$ digit-guess. Trial-subtraction uses [[BinarySubtraction|Ch 4.4.2 subtraction]], continuing the [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4]] **hardware-reuse theme** (addition / subtraction / multiplication / division all built on the same N-bit adder core). Restates **integer-division truncation** explicitly — *"in most languages (for example, C, Python 2, and Java) the fractional portion of the result gets truncated"* — supplying the binary-level mechanism behind the [[IntegerDivision|integer-division]] trap [[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]] flagged at the C-language level; the `%` operator returns the integer remainder ($11 \% 3 = 2$). Worked example $\mathtt{1011}_2 \div \mathtt{11}_2$ (11 ÷ 3) → quotient $\mathtt{0011}_2 = 3$, remainder $\mathtt{10}_2 = 2$. Hardware dividers (restoring / SRT), the [[BitShift|bit-shift]] power-of-two divide shortcut (arithmetic-shift-right), signed-division sign conventions, and division-by-zero trap behaviour are **explicitly out of scope**. ([[dis-4-4-3-mult-div]]).

### Added with [[dis-4-4-2-subtraction]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 4.4.2 Subtraction)

- [Binary Subtraction](concepts/BinarySubtraction.md) — The base-$2$ subtraction operation implemented as **addition of the [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] negation** $A + (-B)$ — *"subtracting $7 - 3$ is equivalent to expressing the operation as $7 + (-3)$"* ([[dis-4-4-2-subtraction|Ch 4.4.2]]). The existing [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]] [[BinaryAddition|adder]] is reused with **one [[XOR|XOR]]-gate row** on operand B (the *flip-all-bits* step) plus **[[CarryIn|`CarryIn`]] = 1** on the LSB adder (the *add one* step), folding the [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] negation into the addition at **zero extra arithmetic hardware**. Mode-switching unifies to one wire `Subtract`: `Subtract = 0` gives ordinary addition ($A + B$), `Subtract = 1` gives subtraction ($A + (\overline{B} + 1) = A - B$). Worked examples $7 - 3 = 4$ and $7 - (-3) = 10$ verify all four sign combinations work via the same circuit (the [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4]] **interpretation-invariance** reapplied). MSB carry-out *"doesn't necessarily indicate overflow"* in subtraction mode — its meaning differs from the addition case; full [[IntegerOverflow|overflow]] rule deferred to a later Ch 4 section. ([[dis-4-4-2-subtraction]]).

### Added with [[dis-4-4-1-addition]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 4.4.1 Addition)

- [Binary Addition](concepts/BinaryAddition.md) — The base-$2$ instantiation of place-value column addition — *the decimal long-addition algorithm transferred to base 2 with only the base changing from $10$ to $2$*. Per [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]], every column's elementary sum `DigitA + DigitB + CarryIn` lies in $\{0,1,2,3\}$, producing a one-bit `Sum` and a one-bit `CarryOut` per the [[FullAdder|full-adder]] truth table (`Sum = XOR`, `CarryOut = majority`). Operationally **simpler than decimal** because the carry is exactly $\{0,1\}$ rather than $0$–$9$. The same $N$-bit adder serves both [[UnsignedInteger|unsigned]] and [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] operands (the [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4]] interpretation-invariance principle); the MSB [[CarryOut|carry-out]] is **silently truncated**, the root mechanism of [[IntegerOverflow|integer overflow]]. ([[dis-4-4-1-addition]]).
- [Carry](concepts/Carry.md) — The bit (or digit, in non-binary bases) that propagates from one column-addition position to the next when the column sum exceeds the base. In [[BinaryAddition|binary addition]] always **exactly $0$ or $1$** — the only multi-bit elementary sum is $1+1=\mathtt{0b10}$. Per [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]], every bit-position adder has a `CarryIn` (from the lower position) and a `CarryOut` (to the higher position), chained ripple-fashion. `CarryIn` is implicit `0` for ordinary addition but **exists architecturally** because [[BinarySubtraction|subtraction]] sets it to `1` to deliver the *add one* in [[TwosComplement|two's complement]]'s *flip-and-add-one* recipe. MSB `CarryOut` truncation = silent overflow; exposed as x86's **CF** flag / ARM's **C** flag. ([[dis-4-4-1-addition]]).

### Added with [[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] (ParProcBook Ch5: Introduction to GPU Programming with CUDA)

- [SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Thread)](concepts/SIMT.md) — NVIDIA's name for the [[Warp|32-thread]] lockstep execution model: same instruction fetched for every thread, divergent threads masked off — the GPU rename of classical [[SIMD]] ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.2.1).
- [Thread Divergence](concepts/ThreadDivergence.md) — When threads in the same [[Warp]] take different branches, the hardware serializes the paths — *"performance killer"* within a warp; **free across warps** ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.2.2).
- [Warp](concepts/Warp.md) — 32-thread SIMT execution unit on NVIDIA GPUs; the latency-hiding unit ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.2.1).
- [Grid (CUDA)](concepts/Grid.md) — Totality of threads for one [[KernelLaunch|kernel launch]]; a 2D arrangement of [[Block|blocks]] ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.4).
- [Block (CUDA)](concepts/Block.md) — Thread group bound to one [[StreamingMultiprocessor|SM]] for the kernel's lifetime; up to 3D, ≤512 threads on Tesla, 128–256 thread rule of thumb ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.4 / §5.6).
- [Kernel Launch (CUDA)](concepts/KernelLaunch.md) — The `kernel<<<grid, block, sharedBytes>>>(args)` syntax; async semantics with `cudaThreadSynchronize` for explicit wait ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.3).
- [Global Memory (CUDA)](concepts/GlobalMemory.md) — Off-chip, app-scope, hundreds-of-cycle latency; the bulk store, mitigated by [[MemoryCoalescing|coalescing]] + [[LatencyHiding|latency hiding]] ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.3.1).
- [Shared Memory (CUDA)](concepts/SharedMemory.md) — On-chip, block-scope, 16K/SM Tesla baseline — *"used essentially as a programmer-managed cache"* ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.3.1).
- [Constant Memory (CUDA)](concepts/ConstantMemory.md) — 64K cached read-from-device-write-from-host tier; populated via `cudaMemcpyToSymbol`; ideal for per-iteration kernel parameters ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.3.5).
- [Texture Memory (CUDA)](concepts/TextureMemory.md) — Cached read-only tier with **2D-aware** caching geometry; suits stencil/image kernels ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.3.5).
- [Unified Memory (CUDA)](concepts/UnifiedMemory.md) — `managed` data with automatic host↔device migration; hardware-assisted from [[NVIDIAPascal|Pascal]] via VM-page-table mechanism; convenience-not-performance ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.17.2).
- [Memory Coalescing (CUDA)](concepts/MemoryCoalescing.md) — Hardware merges half-warp consecutive-word [[GlobalMemory|global-memory]] accesses into one transaction; the headline bandwidth optimization ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.3.2).
- [Loop Unrolling](concepts/LoopUnrolling.md) — Replicating loop bodies for branch elimination + (on GPU) register allocation of small arrays; CUDA exposes `#pragma unroll k` ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.15).
- [CUBLAS](concepts/CUBLAS.md) — NVIDIA's GPU BLAS callable from C; FORTRAN-style column-major; the canonical example: row sums as `cublasSgemv(A * ones)` ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.18.1).
- [CUFFT](concepts/CUFFT.md) — NVIDIA's GPU FFT library; sibling of [[CUBLAS]] ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.18.3).
- [Thrust](concepts/Thrust.md) — C++ STL-style template library for parallel algorithms — uniquely supports **both** [[CUDA]] and [[OpenMP]] backends ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.18.2; deferred to Ch6).
- [Short Vectors (CUDA)](concepts/ShortVectors.md) — `int2`/`int4`/`char2`/etc. packed types treated as single words for memory access; potential 4× bandwidth ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.16).
- [True Caching (CUDA)](concepts/TrueCaching.md) — Newer NVIDIA GPUs split on-chip storage between [[SharedMemory|shared memory]] and an automatic L1 cache; convenience-for-performance tradeoff ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.17.1).
- [Streaming Multiprocessor (SM)](concepts/StreamingMultiprocessor.md) — NVIDIA's multiprocessor unit; contains [[StreamingProcessor|SPs]], schedules [[Warp|warps]] under SIMT, hosts a [[Block|block]] for its lifetime; *"multi-multiprocessor machine"* ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.1).
- [Streaming Processor (SP)](concepts/StreamingProcessor.md) — The individual core inside an [[StreamingMultiprocessor|SM]]; 32-bit word size on Tesla ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.1).
- [OS in Hardware (CUDA)](concepts/OSInHardware.md) — Matloff's framing of the [[StreamingMultiprocessor|SM]]'s warp scheduler as a hardware time-sharer that swaps warps on memory stall — the [[LatencyHiding|latency-hiding]] mechanism ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.2.3).
- [Register Spill](concepts/RegisterSpill.md) — Compiler overflow store for per-thread variables that don't fit in registers; on CUDA, lands in [[GlobalMemory|global memory]] — *"local memory is physically part of global memory"* ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.4.3.5).
- [Atomic Operation (CUDA)](concepts/AtomicOperation.md) — Uninterruptable read-modify-write on global or shared memory (`atomicAdd`, `atomicCAS`, `atomicExch`, ...); the primary inter-block coordination primitive ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.5).
- [atomicAdd (CUDA)](concepts/AtomicAdd.md) — The fetch-and-add atomic; canonical primitive for cross-block reduction (used in the §5.9 mutual-outlinks example) ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.5 / §5.9).
- [cudaThreadSynchronize](concepts/CudaThreadSynchronize.md) — Host-side blocking call that waits for all prior device work; the explicit host barrier and the standard inter-kernel synchronization point ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.3 / §5.5).
- [__syncthreads (CUDA Thread Barrier)](concepts/ThreadBarrier.md) — The intra-[[Block|block]] barrier; **cannot synchronize across blocks** ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.3 / §5.4.3.1 / §5.5).
- [NVIDIA Pascal](concepts/NVIDIAPascal.md) — NVIDIA's 2016 GPU architecture (P100, GTX 10x0); first to provide **hardware-assisted** [[UnifiedMemory]] via VM-page-table mechanism ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.17.2).
- [Functor (Thrust / C++)](concepts/Functor.md) — C++ struct/class with an overloaded `operator()`; carries **state** in its member variables — the property that distinguishes it from a function pointer and the reason Thrust uses functors pervasively ([[parproc-ch06-thrust-programming]] §6.2).
- [Fancy Iterators (Thrust)](concepts/FancyIterator.md) — Umbrella term for [[CountingIterator|counting]] / [[TransformIterator|transform]] / [[ZipIterator|zip]] / [[DiscardIterator|discard]] / [[PermutationIterator|permutation]] iterators — special iterators that virtualize their underlying array to save memory traffic and overhead ([[parproc-ch06-thrust-programming]] §6.8).
- [Counting Iterator (Thrust)](concepts/CountingIterator.md) — Virtual `0, 1, 2, ...` iterator that replaces `thrust::sequence()` without materializing an array; also the idiomatic substrate for `for_each`-as-parallel-loop ([[parproc-ch06-thrust-programming]] §6.8 / §6.9).
- [Transform Iterator (Thrust)](concepts/TransformIterator.md) — Lazy iterator that applies a functor on read; implements **fusion** of `thrust::transform()` into the consuming algorithm via `make_transform_iterator` ([[parproc-ch06-thrust-programming]] §6.8.1).
- [Zip Iterator (Thrust)](concepts/ZipIterator.md) — Co-iterates parallel arrays as tuples; standard idiom for carrying an index alongside a value when composed with a [[CountingIterator|counting iterator]] ([[parproc-ch06-thrust-programming]] §6.8).
- [Discard Iterator (Thrust)](concepts/DiscardIterator.md) — `/dev/null` output iterator for side-effecting `transform()` calls; obviated by `thrust::for_each` for purely side-effecting work ([[parproc-ch06-thrust-programming]] §6.8 / §6.10).
- [Permutation Iterator (Thrust)](concepts/PermutationIterator.md) — Lazy form of [[GatherOperation|`thrust::gather`]]; `*pit == src[map[i]]` computed on read ([[parproc-ch06-thrust-programming]] §6.8).
- [Scatter Operation (Thrust)](concepts/ScatterOperation.md) — Parallel permutation primitive `dst[map[i]] = src[i]`; distinct from Ch1's [[ScatterGather|manager-worker scatter/gather pattern]] ([[parproc-ch06-thrust-programming]] §6.7 / §6.7.1).
- [Gather Operation (Thrust)](concepts/GatherOperation.md) — Parallel permutation primitive `dst[i] = src[map[i]]`; inverse of [[ScatterOperation|scatter]] and the only one of the pair that accepts counting-iterator maps ([[parproc-ch06-thrust-programming]] §6.7 / §6.9).
- [Prefix Scan](concepts/PrefixScan.md) — Running-result parallel primitive (`b_i = a_0 ⊕ ... ⊕ a_i`); `O(log n)` parallel depth via tree-based two-pass algorithm; exposed in Thrust as `inclusive_scan` / `exclusive_scan` ([[parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming]] §5.11 / [[parproc-ch06-thrust-programming]] §6.11).
- [STL for GPU](concepts/STLForGPU.md) — The design pattern Thrust embodies: transplant the C++ STL's containers + iterators + algorithms + function objects onto parallel substrates so the same source compiles to CUDA, OpenMP, or TBB ([[parproc-ch06-thrust-programming]] §6 intro).
- [Hypercube](concepts/Hypercube.md) — 1980s–90s parallel-machine topology — a **d-cube** of $D = 2^d$ PEs with **bit-flip neighbors** (PE $(c_{d-1},...,c_0)$'s ith neighbor flips bit i; d neighbors per PE; max d hops); inductive *duplicate-and-prefix* construction; sub-cube / root / partner formalism; commercially extinct (Intel, nCube/Oracle) but algorithms remain influential — [[MPI]] collectives still use logical-hypercube schedules ([[parproc-ch07-message-passing-systems]] §7.2).
- [Network of Workstations (NOW)](concepts/NetworkOfWorkstations.md) — Commodity-PC message-passing substrate; *"the network is literally the weakest link"*; Ch7 explicitly retires *NOW* as a term, replacing it with [[Cluster]]; modern NOWs are hybrid (multi-core nodes → pure MPI or MPI+OpenMP); positioned as the *economic* answer to the [[Hypercube|hypercube]] market collapse + shared-memory-hardware expense ([[parproc-ch07-message-passing-systems]] §7.3).
- [Infiniband](concepts/Infiniband.md) — Switch-based [[NetworkOfWorkstations|NOW]] interconnect with **RDMA** (eliminates the app↔OS-space copy), 1.0–3.0 μs [[Latency]], 1.0–2.0 GB/s [[Bandwidth]], 5–10% CPU usage, 3–5 μs atomic-op latency, true hardware multicast; building block is a switch *"similar in concept to [[OmegaNetwork|Ω-net]]"*; the *"MPI_Bcast is O(P) sequential sends unless your hardware + MPI build support multicast"* warning lives here ([[parproc-ch01-intro-parallel-processing]] / [[parproc-ch07-message-passing-systems]] §7.3.1).
- [SPMD (Single Program Multiple Data)](concepts/SPMD.md) — The execution model behind [[MPI]] — every node runs the *same compiled program* on *different data partitions*, branching by rank with `if (me == 0) ...`; distinct from [[SIMD]] (per-instruction lockstep) and from MPMD (different binaries per node); [[CUDA]] is SPMD-at-thread-level + SIMD-at-warp-level ([[parproc-ch08-introduction-to-mpi]] §8.1.2).
- [Collective Communication](concepts/CollectiveCommunication.md) — The class of [[MPI]] primitives where *all nodes in a communicator participate simultaneously*; *"all the nodes in the group execute this line. The only difference is the action; most nodes participate by receiving, while node 0 participates by sending."* (§8.6.2); seven named ops ([[MPIBcast|Bcast]] / [[MPIReduce|Reduce]] / [[MPIAllreduce|Allreduce]] / [[MPIGather|Gather]] / [[MPIAllgather|Allgather]] / [[MPIScatter|Scatter]] / [[MPIBarrier|Barrier]]); guarantees are semantic, performance is conditional on hardware-multicast / RDMA / [[Hypercube|hypercube-style]] recursive-doubling schedules ([[parproc-ch08-introduction-to-mpi]] §8.6 / [[parproc-ch07-message-passing-systems]] §7.3.1).
- [MPI_Send](concepts/MPISend.md) — [[MPI]]'s fundamental point-to-point send — six-argument signature `(buf, count, datatype, dest, tag, comm)`; *"safe to overwrite the send buffer"* return semantic — **not** *"receiver has the data"*; typed messages exist as a **heterogeneity broker** for endianness (Intel little-endian vs Sun SPARC big-endian) + 32-vs-64-bit word width ([[parproc-ch08-introduction-to-mpi]] §8.3.3.3).
- [MPI_Recv](concepts/MPIRecv.md) — The matching point-to-point receive — seven args (six match send + output `MPI_Status` struct); wildcards `MPI_ANY_SOURCE` / `MPI_ANY_TAG` recoverable via `status.MPI_SOURCE` / `status.MPI_TAG`; variable-length receives use `MPI_Get_count(&status, type, &actual_count)`; always blocks until matching message arrives; on TCP/IP requires an OS-buffer → app-buffer copy [[Infiniband]] RDMA eliminates ([[parproc-ch08-introduction-to-mpi]] §8.3.3.4 / §8.4 / §8.7.1).
- [MPI_Bcast](concepts/MPIBcast.md) — One-to-all [[CollectiveCommunication|collective]] broadcast `(buffer, count, datatype, root, comm)`; *"all the nodes in the group execute this line"* (§8.6.2) — replaces a hand-rolled `if (me == 0) for (i=1; i<nnodes; i++) MPI_Send(...) else MPI_Recv(...)` loop; performance ranges from O(P) (linear-send fallback) to O(log P) (binomial tree) to O(1) (hardware multicast) depending on MPI build + fabric ([[parproc-ch08-introduction-to-mpi]] §8.6.2).
